utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the witness to enter the court, I wanted to inform you and to request that if Witness Stojanovic does not complete his testimony today -- well, we'll complete the examination-in-chief, but there's always the possibility that the cross-examination will not be completed today. In that case, I want like to ask that in Monday we interrupt his examination, because we have the next witness coming in, who is Dikovic, Ljubisa Dikovic, and from the Ministry of Defence he has been authorised to be absent from work just for two days, because he is otherwise engaged at his job. If you agree. Now, we wanted to bring him in earlier on, and the Prosecution complained they didn't have enough time to prepare, and since he was on our notification list from October saying he would testify in December, we're bringing him in, in the last week to avoid any complaints from the Prosecution, but as I say, he cannot be here after Monday and Tuesday because he has to get back to his job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It should be to possible to accommodate that, but I'd be surprised if we did not complete Mr. Stojanovic today, if your estimate of the time likely to be taken is accurate. So let's crack on and see if we can't solve the problem the simple way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. Yesterday we were going to show the video clip. So if you agree, we'll carry on with that straight away. And we disclosed it to the Prosecution yesterday. I hope they have no objection. So perhaps we could deal with that first and then continue on as planned, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the examination by Mr. Bakrac will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth, which you gave at the beginning of your evidence will continue to apply to your evidence throughout. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at Exhibit 5D1376. That is an exhibit that was not on the 65 ter list. We announced it yesterday, and it is up to you to decide whether to admit it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp does not seem to object now, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, look at this video footage and tell us when we finish if that is what you told us about yesterday concerning the visit to Batusa village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While we are waiting, could I just indicate that while I didn't object to the video, I -- I would have objected, but it's probably too late now, to counsel telling the witness what is on the video, instead of asking the witness if he could tell us what the witness depicts -- what the video depicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your comment is noted, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Bakrac, 1376 is the correct number, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is how I -- 1376.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have we seen enough, Mr. Bakrac? Because we're not hearing anything, and if there's anything else to see, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in a few seconds it will be over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, before proceeding, Your Honour did indicate that you're not hearing anything, and there now arises some difficulties. One of the problems of trying to be agreeable when things are done in haste is that sometimes we're cross -- at cross-wires because the type I got late last night did not have sound. I'm hearing sound now, but it appears that the Bench is not hearing any sound. And I don't know if the exhibit proposed is the video with sound, as I'm hearing it now, which is not what I got last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you'd allowed me to clarify the position, we have heard nothing. This is simply pictures, as far as the Bench is concerned. No doubt Mr. Bakrac is going to ask the witness to explain what it was. We'll get to that in a moment, because 5D1376, according to the records, is a report dated the 19th of January, 1999 and is not a video clip. It's a report by Colonel Jelic to the Pristina Corps Command. Now, you can sort that out later and you can deal with it at the break and -- and clarify the position with everyone and for the record. Let's now proceed with what question you wish to ask based on this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, my learned friend Mr. Stamp objected that I led you as to what this is about. Is it mentioned anywhere in the text which village this was going on in, the name of the village?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the video-clip you've just seen, you could see the final talks with the locals in Batusa village in Djakovica municipality that took place in a local schoolhouse close to a brook. And in this video footage you could see the man I talked about yesterday, Zejnil Batusa, the most influential and senior man of that village, who was sitting next to General Pavkovic. And you could see the most prominent people there, the seniors. Let me just say about this footage it might seem odd to an uninformed viewer that the villagers are sitting on the floor, that is, according to their ancient custom; whereas, the representatives of the army are sitting on chairs. I and General Pavkovic and the others wanted to sit down on the floor with them, but the Albanians would not agree to that. They brought some chairs instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind us of the date of this, please. Let's concentrate on what really matters here. We know that Albanians sit on the floor. What -- when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it was sometime in May 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've got to finish your evidence today, so let's concentrate on the questions that are being asked. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to move on now. I think what we have seen is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just tell us what happened. I mean, what were you discussing at the meeting? This point -- we did not get a translation of what was being said, so tell us what -- you may have heard it, although the sound was very dim, but we need to know what you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the locals of the said village were complaining to the members of the army that every night they were being disturbed by terrorists from the neighbouring village of Junik, who came to their village threatening them unless they accepted weapons, to join staff, that they are taking away some certain -- some young men to join their staffs. And on the road that goes from their village to Kosare border post, they felt unsafe and they wanted the protection of the army. These were talks, negotiations between the villagers and the members of the army, and it was agreed that the army would give protection to that village, and in exchange the locals of that village would not join the terrorist staffs of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This was in May 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let us go on now. In practical terms, were there any restricting factors in the work of security organs and the military police after the beginning of the NATO aggression? And during that aggression?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. War is certainly not something natural and the security organs and the military police faced numerous problems from the very outset. I said yesterday the greatest problem was the beginning of massive migration of the Albanian population. And as for the work of security organs of the Pristina Corps itself, I want to emphasise that under very complex security conditions, they had to discharge their prescribed functions and act according to regulations, and in doing their duty, they often risked their lives. I also want to stress that part of my security organs got killed while performing their duties, such as chief of security of the 549th Brigade, Vlado Mikicevic, head of the Tactical Group 252, Albanian terrorists in the area of Bajgora, to the north-east of Kosovska Mitrovica, kidnapped one whole vehicle holding one commanding officer and four other officers who were on their way to perform an on-site investigation. After month-long negotiations with the help of the OSCE mission,, we managed to free some of them. One part of our department for combatting crime were wounded on duty. A great problem was frequent relocation of units, problems with communications, bombing day and night, difficult access to witnesses that we had to contact on instructions of the prosecutor, primarily witnesses of Albanian ethnicity. When I say this, I mean first and foremost witnesses and injured parties in rape crimes, where we did not manage to elicit their cooperation, that was made difficult by their ancient customs of Albanians and their beliefs. Within the unit itself, we had difficulties because of the reluctance to report on colleagues. All this made the work of security organs in 1998 [as interpreted] and 1999 very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe "1998" should not be in the transcript. The witness only said "1999" and my question only had to do with 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did security organs and the military police in 1999 have any information that certain members of the corps committed various criminal offences, especially serious crimes, such as murder, rape, inhumane treatment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The organs of military security of the Pristina Corps had such information in 1999. For all such crimes, security organs took the prescribed legal steps and all the crimes that we were informed of were prosecuted before the competent authorities; that is to say, we filed criminal reports to the competent prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that, would you clarify something and tell us what the duties of the security organs are and the military police when they receive information that a crime had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those duties are prescribed by law, the Law on Criminal Procedure. And I said yesterday that the security organs of the military police have the right and duty and authorisation from the authorised organs within the internal affairs organs, and those tasks relate first and foremost to the following: That upon learning that a crime had taken place, they must inform the senior officer, and all measures must be taken to secure the site, not to destroy or hide any traces of the crime, and to uncover the perpetrator or prevent the perpetrator from escaping, to collect the necessary evidence, and then to inform the investigative organs and the organs of the military police, who would then carry out an investigation. And I wish to stress here that whenever a crime is committed, a serious crime, the crime of murder or a crime which results in death that, the investigating judge of the military court in question would go out on the scene of the crime to investigate and inspect it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you perform all those duties, is that where the duty of the organs, military police organs and everyone else ends in documenting the case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The military police security organs continue to investigate. They investigate the circumstances and collect the necessary information, proof, and evidence that the crime had been committed, and also act pursuant to the orders issued and guide-lines issued by the prosecutor; that is to say, to take witnesses, take statements from witnesses, and everything that will throw light on the crime that was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, when the perpetrator of a criminal crime hands himself up or comes into the hands of the organs, does your -- do your duties stop there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All further work is just executed pursuant to instructions given by the prosecutor in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, at the material time when the NATO bombings started and when the war started, indeed, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, did you have information according to which certain commanders on the ground failed to report to the corps command about crimes committed by members of their units or that crime -- they tried to cover up crimes like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Individual commanders did -- didn't -- did not have -- we did not have any information like that; that is to say, that the commanders would cover up crimes committed, cover them up from their superior commands, but we did have knowledge and information that individual commanders of the units in question were not informed that in their units there were people who had committed criminal -- crimes or offences. And the information came from the security organs of the military police. But on a regular basis, they would then inform the commanders in question of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, your service, did it have information to the effect that certain corps members committed mass crimes? Was anything like that reported?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs of the Pristina Corps did not have information according to which certain units committed any mass crimes, but they did -- information did reach them that in certain locations when the army units arrived, that either individually or in groups there were bodies found, dead bodies. Now, for all such cases, the corps command, up the chain of command, and indeed the security organs of the military police and investigating judge, would go on the spot, on site, to investigate any such cases and the circumstances thereof. Now, if dead bodies were found in certain locations, the security organs would then take measures to collect the necessary information and evidence, and then this would help the crime to be prosecuted, the perpetrators to be prosecuted. I'm speaking about the locations where it was established that army units had been in place. Now, about the other localities, localities where we were not able to establish that there were any members of units or where there were no combat activities going on, then we would inform the competent organs of the Ministry of the Interior about such locations and such crimes and the military prosecutor, which by virtue of his duty would then go on to inform the territorially -- the territorial military prosecutors in charge. Now, for localities where we were not able to establish whether there were or were not any army units present or whether there was or was not combat in those localities, we would take all the necessary investigative steps, on-site investigation, filing criminal reports against perpetrators, and then the activities would carry on to collect the evidence, as is normal in any such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I don't think we have it on record -- or rather, I think you said -- or rather, would you repeat. If you didn't know who the perpetrator was, what criminal reports would you file? Against whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the localities where we did not know for sure, where we were not able to establish with certainty whether in those locations there had been any combat conducted by army units, in such cases we would take all the necessary investigative measures, or on-site investigations, and then criminal reports would be filed against person or persons unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the basis of your operative work and collection of evidence, later on were any cases taken to court? Were they prosecuted, that had been -- criminal reports filed against person or persons unknown, after the end of the war, when the war was over?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. For example, the case was resolved of the killing of six civilians in the village of Gornja Klina, in the municipality of Srbica, where it was established -- criminal responsibility was established against Lieutenant-Colonel Slobodan Stocic, and then criminal responsibility once again for a group of volunteers was established in the 175th Motorised Brigade in the village of Zegra, in -- on the territory of the municipality of Gnjilane, with Vlado Zmajevic, a volunteer at the head, and he was also prosecuted. And we were able to throw light on the crime that had taken place in the municipality of Slovinje, the municipality of Lipljan, actually, those proceedings are underway; but the perpetrators of that crime are in custody and court proceedings are underway. And there are numerous other examples that I could quote as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, how can you from this distance of time appraise the efficiency of the security organs that you led or the military police during the war in Kosovo and Metohija in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under existing conditions -- or rather, the conditions that existed as I described them a moment ago, and in a relatively short period of time -- because I wish to stress that we are dealing with a period -- a three-month period, which is how long the state of war went on. With all the necessary limitations, my assessment is that the security organs of the military police were highly efficacious. They did their job very professionally in documenting and prosecuting all illegal acts and all perpetrators. I would like to stress on this occasion that just during the war the security organs, the military police received 250 criminal reports for serious crimes that were committed, including the crimes of violating the provisions of international humanitarian law and war law. Of those 250 cases, as far as I can remember, some 20 or 22 cases were crimes, and after the war, the military courts received another 100 criminal reports for various crimes and offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, in English a number of times the expression "the security organs of the military police" has been used. Is that, in fact, the expression that's being used?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Security organs and the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you said that 20 to 22 cases -- ah, right. It says "crimes." You said "crimes." What did you mean when you said "crimes"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the crime of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What was the cooperation between the military security service and the MUP and state security during 1999 in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, cooperation between the security organs of the Pristina Corps and the military police, with the organs of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and the State Security Service, was very proper and correct and was based on regular exchanges of information, both orally and in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The organs and units of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia in Kosovo and Metohija during 1999, were they subordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia -- or rather, the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organs of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia during 1999 were not subordinated to the command of the Pristina Corps. I do know that sometime in mid-April - I think it was on the 20th of April - an order reached me from the command of the 3rd Army which referred to a Supreme Command Staff order, by which the organs and units of the Ministry of the Interior in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija be re-subordinated to the command of the Pristina Corps. I also know of another instance, that the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic, was informed in writing from the subordinated commander -- the commanders of subordinated units that the organs of the Ministry of the Interior refused to be re-subordinated to army units, claiming that that order, which was signed by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, General Ojdanic, was not binding upon them but that it -- it was the order that they would receive down the vertical chain of command that would be binding, from their own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, was there any information about any bad cooperation or poor cooperation and work between individual units and MUP organs at lower levels? Any poor examples?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were during the wartime conditions, well, not any drastic examples or drastic problems, but the -- the major problem was, as far as I can remember, this: Cooperation between the command of the 37th Motorised Brigade, for example, and the chief of the internal affairs department in Glogovac, and those complaints related to mutual duties and responsibilities and taking measures to sanitize the -- the terrain after combat and fighting against the Siptar terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what was done in such cases? What did the corps command do when faced with a problem like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in all cases, as indeed in this one, the corps command on a regular basis was interested in promoting cooperation; that is to say, between the Ministry of the Interior and the army; that it should be kept at a proper level, because the situation was otherwise highly complex. So if there were any problems that cropped up at a local level, lower level down the chain of command, both in the army and in MUP, with respect to coordination and collaboration, it would send command organs in the specific case -- if you're asking me about that, I know, for instance, that the corps command sent Colonel Paprica and Colonel Radojko Stefanovic, the chief of the department for operations in the corps command, to see what was going on, what was happening with this operation between the 37th Motorised Brigade and the Glogovac MUP representative. And then the corps commander sent me down there with a team, and on the 7th of May I also went down there to investigate these allegations. And when we talked to the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade and with the chief of the department of interior -- of the interior of the MUP of Serbia in Glogovac, and when we pointed out to them their responsibilities and tasks with respect to sanitizing the terrain and mutual cooperation -- well, that's what we did. We pointed that out to them. And I think that in the second half of May, once again, pursuant to an order from the commander I went down on the ground to deal with those problems and resolve them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, what were the duties of the members of the Army of Yugoslavia with respect to regulating and controlling the security regime in the territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security regime and the duties of the members of the Army of Yugoslavia in that respect -- well, the Army of Yugoslavia had no duties to regulate the security regime on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija; however, it did have duties and responsibilities to regulate the security regime in the area of deployment of its units. And to regulate the security regime on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, it was our organs who were in charge. First and foremost, the organs of the Ministry of the Interior, the State Security Service, the local self-government authorities, and as I say, they were different organs who were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let's take a look at -- now at Exhibit -- Defence Exhibit 5D382, please. And we'd like to hear your comments, briefly. Or would you, rather, look at para 3 on page 1. Tell us, why did the army have its own check-point in that village when you said the army was not in charge of enforcing security in that territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army had its check-point in Klokote village, Vitina municipality, on the road from Vitina to Gnjilane, because 30 metres away from that check-point there was the command post of 175th Infantry Brigade. Such check-points were set up by other units as well in their areas of deployment, or in the immediate vicinity of their areas of deployment, with a view to preventing uncontrolled entry or exit from areas of deployment of units. Let me give you one of the practical reasons. Uncontrolled movement of soldiers or conscripts could not be allowed lest they go absent without official leave. These check-points were manned by military police, and each of these check-points covered the area of deployment of the respective unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let us now look at para 4. Look carefully and tell us, did military police overstep their authority in this case? Then I'll have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think they overstepped their authority in this specific case. They simply assisted the Ministry of Interior organs, because the crime took place in the immediate vicinity of their check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of this para 4, we see that two recruits, Vladica Djurasevic and Dejan Stojkovic entered the house of two old women of Serb ethnicity in Klokote village, and at gunpoint robbed them of 1300 Swiss francs. Were there other such cases where military conscripts committed crimes not only against Albanian civilians but also at Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We see from this document that two recruits robbed at gunpoint two Serb old women. Do you know, were there any other examples where members of the army perpetrated offences and crimes against Serb civilians as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, speaking of crimes such as robbery, theft, or looting, members of the army committed them against Albanian and Serb civilians alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, look at the last paragraph of this para 4. Tell us, was there an attempted rape -- and from the name of the injured party, would it be a Serb woman?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean para 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, the last paragraph of para 4.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, would you tell you something about para 5 as well. Why did military police intervene in this case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, the military police acted appropriately, because as we can see, these perpetrators of extortion were wearing camouflage uniforms, so that at the time they intervened, the military police could not know whether they were army members or policemen. So after taking them into custody and processing them duly, they turned them over to the competent authorities. As soon as the perpetrators were wearing camouflage uniform, it falls within the jurisdiction of the military police, and in this case military police were right to react the way they did. In this specific case, the perpetrators turned out to be civilians, and they were therefore turned over to the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at another document, 5D991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Look at the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you deal with that document, you -- you've been talking about the responsibility of the military security organs for security in the area of deployment of VJ units. We've had some evidence earlier in the case, in fact, this week, about the technical definition of what's called "the area of responsibility" and also "the area of defence." Is that something -- are these concepts different from "the area of deployment" that you've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area of responsibility is a broader concept than "the area of deployment." The area of responsibility is a territory delimited by four points within which the unit performs certain activities or actions; whereas, the area of deployment is the area in which the elements of the battle order are positioned. And in that area the unit does not perform any activities. That's the command post, communications centre, command organs, et cetera. It's a narrower field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Look in the last paragraph and tell us, as before, whether they were right to do what they did. The last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Members of 180th Military Territorial Detachment acted appropriately and -- according to the law, and later over -- later turned over the persons concerned to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So this citizen who set fire to houses, and he was caught doing that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that it's clear that it's one person who is concerned. Now, I'd like to know: Did you hear about the term "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" while you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did you hear and in which context?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the term "Joint Command," to the best of my recollection, sometime in mid-June 1998 from the chief of operations of the command of the Pristina Corps, Colonel Milan Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What did he say to you on that occasion? How did you come to learn of this term?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that -- let me just give you a brief context. On orders of the corps commander, I had to keep a working map in the security organ of the Pristina Corps where we drew all the information about the plans and intentions and locations and positions of Albanian terrorists. And it was my duty to submit this information to the chief of operations, Colonel Djakovic, every day. I said yesterday that after the OSCE mission arrived I also had the obligation to submit this information regularly to the head of the liaison team for the OSCE mission. When sharing this information with Colonel Djakovic, I heard from him this term, "Joint Command." I asked him what it meant. And as he explained to me then, that term referred to the joint meetings of representatives of the Pristina Corps Command and the Ministry of the Interior to exchange information and to coordinate cooperation and coordinated actions between the army and the MUP behind the lines. He often stressed that it was a problem that the information that the corps command receives down the vertical chain of command - that is to say, orders - and the orders that the MUP receive down their own chain of command consistently failed to deal with the problem on the ground of properly coordinating the actions of the army, on one side, and the MUP, on the other side in a specific operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you ever attend such a meeting or briefing?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean a meeting of that Joint Command? No, I never, never attended any meetings that somebody termed "the Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Djakovic tell you where those meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Colonel Djakovic did not tell me where those meetings took place, but from what I was able to learn from persons who worked on the security detail of the corps commander, those coordination meetings were sometimes held in the building of the Ministry of the Interior and, at other times, in the building of the Executive Council of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did these meetings of the Joint Command take any decisions as to how to use the units of the corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no way. In view of my position and duties, I would have had to know about that. Decisions were taken down the prescribed chain of command in the army, as far as army units are concerned, and I believe it worked the same way in the Ministry of the Interior; although, I don't know about them. However, the corps command received all orders on how to use its units from the forward command post of the 3rd Army that was located in the Kosovo Heroes Barracks in Pristina. And I know that at that command post there was either the Chief of Staff or the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell me, now when you are telling us this, what year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're a -- a very experienced army officer and had served by 1999 for six years in Kosovo? During the period prior to 1998, were you familiar with the concept of coordinating action between the VJ and the MUP to deal with problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. From March 1998 onwards, March, April, and May, numerous problems manifested themselves, because in that period MUP units suffered significant losses at their check-points on roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand -- I understand all that, but my question's a different one. Prior to 1998, just in the ordinary course of your service as an army officer, were you aware of situations in which there was coordinated action between the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before 1998 the security situation in Kosovo was much more peaceful. But even then there was coordination and cooperation between members of the army and the MUP, and this cooperation consisted in an exchange of information, resulting from the monitoring of the overall security situation, and at that time there was no need for any anti-terrorist operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What type of cooperation was then required when things were peaceful in this area between VJ and between the MUP? What -- can you kindly elucidate what kind of cooperation you had? I mean, more than living together, what sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before 1998, if I understood your question correctly, the cooperation consisted mainly of informing each other and exchanging information about the overall security situation in Kosovo. Second, it had to deal with specific issues of cooperation between competent Secretariats of Internal Affairs and specific commands on the same level, be it in Djakovica or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I go on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did it seem odd to you when you heard from Colonel Djakovic about that term, "Joint Command," did you ask him what it meant?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not appear odd to me at all, because from what I had seen and the information that I was providing to him about the activities of Albanian terrorists, which I suppose he shared with MUP organs and the State Security Service, and I also suppose they shared their information with him about the plans and activities of Albanian terrorists, I knew that there were certain problems concerning coordination, cooperation, and coordinated actions between MUP and army at lower levels, as to a soldier and member of the collegium of the corps command, it was quite clear to me that that command did not have any prerogatives of a proper command, in terms of decision-making or issuing orders. I knew that in practice that's not the way it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, do you have any knowledge to the effect that such meetings were held in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In view of the position you occupied, would you have had to have known, had meetings taken place in 1999? Must you have known about them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly I would have to have known about them, had there been such meetings in 1999, but I would have had to know in 1998 as well that there was some sort of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, General, what I'm asking you is this: You say, no, there were no such meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in 1999 there, weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that you would have had to have known, in view of the function you performed, about those meetings, had they taken place?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I must have known, since I was the assistant commander. So I would have had to have known. I would have had certain duties and responsibilities for the commander's security, in order to undertake other measures. It was a state of war, after all. And in a war, faced with a situation of war, all the movements of the commander, the military police security organs always have duties, and this is defined in the regulations of the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Going back to 1998, I -- I have formed the impression that the only source of your knowledge of the Joint Command was Djakovic. Are you saying that you had other knowledge of it and its meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, as the chief of the security organ, I certainly had several -- lots of information and knowledge, and I would certainly have known about that, had something like that existed, in the figurative sense, Djakovic or -- I don't know who referred to this as "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't know if it's translation, but you're not -- you're not dealing with the question I've proposed in English. I want to know if you have another source of information about the Joint Command in 1998 other than Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had -- well, from the immediate security of the commander, security detail of the commander, the corporals, where they go, some other information, sergeants or something like that, telling me where they were going, but not other information. I just was told where the commander was going, what his movements were. So after going to the forward command post, for example, in the Kosovski Junaci barracks, the forward command post of the 3rd Army at about 1800 hour, he would report on his proposals and the 3rd Army command would verify a decision of his or he would go to the Ministry of the Interior, for instance, or to the executive council building. So I would just ask where he was going, what his movements were, and I was explained that he was going to dovetail the orders received with the MUP organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't -- that doesn't suggest that there is either a -- a body or a concept known as "the Joint Command." And I hope I'm not misrepresenting the evidence from earlier in the case, but -- but Mr. Lazarevic, in giving evidence, certainly, I think, gave us the impression that it would not be unusual for him not to know where his commander, General Pavkovic, was going on any particular day. He was not his brother's keeper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're talking about 1998. Lazarevic was at the forward command post, and he testified about that throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But there were occasions when he might have been expected to know where his commander was, and -- and I think it's an accurate recollection of the evidence that he was not able to -- it was -- it was not unusual for -- for him not to be aware of -- of that. Now, what I'm trying to understand is why you say in 1999, if there was any meeting that was termed, a Joint Command meeting, you were bound to know about it. I'm not understanding that point at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's try and clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, what did you mean to say when you said that? Perhaps at the very outset we passed this over too quickly. But in 1999, in view of the position you held, did you engage some members of the military police to provide security for the commander attending those meetings or for going to those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understood you to say the following: Well, it is not the corps commander who has to know. He need not know where the commander of the army is, but the chief of security must know where his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've misunderstood me. I was talking about the situation when Mr. Lazarevic was Chief of Staff and Mr. Pavkovic was head of the Pristina Corps and there were occasions when he would go to -- General Pavkovic would go to meetings and Mr. Lazarevic would not necessarily know where he was. Now, what I'm trying to understand is why you should know where General Pavkovic or General Lazarevic were at any given time in 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, I understand your question. I wouldn't need to know at each point in time where my commander is. There was no need for that. It is the people providing security for him that needed to know that. But my answer was this: In 1999, had there been any meetings which would be termed here "Joint Command meetings," then I would have had to have some assignment for additional security or other responsibilities towards the corps commander. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in 1998 that wasn't the case, so why should it be different in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, simply, Mr. President, because in 1999 there was a war on and the corps commanders -- the corps commander was especially in jeopardy. We looked into the possibility of him being kidnapped, captured, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You've clarified that now. Just a brief question. During the war, the corps commander, did he go to attend any meetings in Belgrade? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Pristina Corps, you mean? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. He never went to attend any meetings in -- to Belgrade in the course of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let's move on to another area now. And tell me this: You -- or rather, your security organ - that is to say, of the Pristina Corps- during 1999, were you controlled or toured by representatives of the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During 1999, on two occasions the security department of the Pristina Corps was inspected and controlled by the top-level leaders from the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff. The first time an inspection of the work of the security organs of the Pristina Corps, was done at the end of April, when the chief of the security department, General Geza Farkas came on tour to inspect. The second time the Pristina Corps security organs were toured by the deputy chief of the security administration, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, the assistant chief of the security administration, General Branko Gajic, and the chief of the department of security of the 3rd Army, Colonel Stojadin Antic. And I think this was from the 1st to the 6th or the 1st to the 7th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, tell me, please, the work of the security service, your security service, when the first inspection was conducted, how did General Farkas assess the work of your security service after his first inspection?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the chief myself - and the meeting was attended by all subordinate chiefs of the security organs units as well - I briefed General Farkas on the overall situation in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and the measures and steps taken by the security organs of the military police and also the results achieved, the results of their work to document and put a stop to unlawful activities. General Farkas, for his part, on that occasion assessed highly the work of the security organs of the Pristina Corps and military police. He used the term -- or he said that they were the -- sowing the seeds of new cadres and young people for the security service. And when we briefed him and when he spoke to us, he said that the organs of the military security service, 95 per cent of the time, had documented and prevented any unlawful activities. And that was high recognition indeed for us. After General Farkas did his tour and inspection, on the 13th of May, which is otherwise celebrated or once was celebrated as the day of the military service, or Military Service Day, the corps commander, when he heard this, promoted a number of officers from the security service ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, tell me, please -- or rather, you've already said this. You've already told us, when General Vasiljevic arrived for an inspection with his team. On that occasion, did General Vasiljevic tell you the reasons for his visit and his inspection, him and his team, of course?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic told me that he had come on a regular tour to tour the organs of security of the Pristina Corps on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell me, what units on that occasion did they visit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my proposal - and General Vasiljevic accepted my proposal. And together with him there was General Gajic and Colonel Antic. We toured the units up at the front line, the front lines of defence facing the Republic of Albania. We also inspected the security organs of the 37th Motorised Brigade in Glogovac, the security organs of the 125th Motorised Brigade not at their command post but the security organ was in a village called Vitomirica near Pec. Then we inspected the security organs in the Djakovica barracks and the security organs of the 549th Motorised Brigade at the Prizren garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The chiefs of the security organs of those particular units, did they brief them? Did they report to them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The security organs of the units mentioned did brief the representatives of the Supreme Command -- of the security administration of the situation in the field, in the units, the measures they had taken, and they raised some of the problems they had encountered during their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, how did General Vasiljevic and his team appraise the work, if they did, of the units after having heard briefings and touring and inspecting these units? How did they assess the work of your security service?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, with his team, spent five or six days in the field. He had an opportunity of learning about the work of the security organs in detail. And when he finished his tour, he expressed his satisfaction with everything he'd seen and with everything that the military police organs did. And when we travelled around and toured these units, a NATO plane chased us and we had to get away from that. I don't want to tire the Court with the problems. But he said, "How can you survive at all under such conditions, let alone achieving the results you've achieved?" That was his comment and observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, during the time of General Vasiljevic's visit, can you remember whether you attended with him any meeting at which there were representatives of the MUP present and some other state functionaries, state officials?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic was in the area of deployment of the security section of the Pristina Corps all the time with his associates. He stayed there. He reported there. He lived there. He ate there. And with General Vasiljevic, I attended one meeting, and I think that was in the afternoon sometime, when I was called by the corps commander to come to the information centre of the Pristina Corps Command to attend a meeting there, and I said that General Vasiljevic was in the area, and so he told me to bring General Vasiljevic along too. So we went together to this meeting at the Hotel Grand in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, who invited you to attend the meeting at the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavkovic invited us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say "the Grand Hotel," the information centre there, was the Pristina Corps Command put up there too?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. And I stressed yesterday that the Pristina Corps Command was dispersed in the broader area around Pristina and that the locations were changed frequently. If you wanted -- if you want to give me the locations. But in the Grand Hotel, the informations centre was located there, where persons were exchanged for subordinate units, and the information centre was the -- dealt with the care and attention of soldiers informing their families about the fate of their soldiers where their soldiers where and what had happened to them. And sometimes parents would come there too trying to find their children who were soldiers in the area, to talk to them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, tell me, if you can remember, and to the best of your recollections, who attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the meeting at the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When General Pavkovic -- no, I mean General Vasiljevic and I arrived there, we entered into the premises of the information centre. We found sitting there General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic. They were already there. And then also present was the chief of the state security sector for Kosovo and Metohija, Mr. Misa Vilotic, and also present was Mr. -- or rather, the representative of MUP, General Lukic. And later on - he was a little late - General Kovacevic arrived. He was the chief of the armoured mechanised units in the Supreme Command Staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any state officials?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were sitting down, Mr. Sainovic came in and Mr. Andjelkovic, president of the Executive Council of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija, and they sat down at the same table as General Pavkovic and Lazarevic. It was a small area. We were sitting next to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you remember, what was the talk about at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole meeting was very short. I think 10 to 15 minutes. My general impression from that meeting was that the atmosphere was troubled, unpleasant. But General Pavkovic addressed us and said that Mr. Sainovic had arrived from Belgrade wishing to inform us of the long-standing negotiations between the president of Yugoslavia and the intermediaries, the Troika, headed by Mr. Ate Sare [phoen]. After that, Mr. Sainovic addressed us, sharing with us that the agreement between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the international community would be signed very soon, that that agreement envisages a cease-fire and a withdrawal of the army and the MUP from Kosovo and Metohija, and that very, very soon withdrawal would start so that all activities should be terminated as soon as possible. It was a very troubled situation. Everybody was taken by surprise and taken aback. And I believe General Lazarevic said on that occasion, "What am I supposed to do now when I have already started some activities against terrorist strongholds in certain locations?" I believe he mentioned Jablanica. Then General Lukic said that he had some ongoing activities too. And to that Mr. Sainovic replied, "I don't know. You see, all that has to be finalised, brought to an end. The agreement is about to be signed, and it envisages a withdrawal of the army and the police from Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What Mr. Sainovic said, was it an order or --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no order. It was a statement of fact or a suggestion. He said, once again, "It may have been signed already, as I'm speaking. If it's not, it will be signed soon, and withdrawal is forthcoming, very soon. You have to see what you are going to do about your activities that are still underway."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we now look together at 5D236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, that -- that night, did you have dinner at the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I have also to ask: When these two generals were talking in that meeting, explaining that they have started some activities against, what they call as, terrorists, and Mr. Stojanovic said, Now they have to put an end to that in view of the treaty which is to come about. Did they elaborate? Did they speak more about what activities they have started? I mean, did they mention about those activities to tell Mr. Sainovic that they were ahead with those activities and will it now be proper to stop those? Did they elaborate? Did they speak more about those activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, they said no more. They just said that they had some activities that were ongoing. They did not speak at length to Mr. Sainovic about them. I believe Mr. Lazarevic mentioned Jablanica and General Lukic also said that there were some activities going on in another location. They did not elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let us now look at this exhibit. It's also about the meeting. Can we see page 4 in B/C/S, para 4, "State of morale." And could you please look at the last-but-one sentence in this combat report. It begins with the words "over the past 24 hours." Is that the place where you said you attended a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document shows what I said earlier: "Over the past 24 hours, the information centre received 197 calls from parents and family of the members of our units." This shows the great interest parents had in the safety of their children in that very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But that information centre is the room you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, please look at the next page, para 6, "Commanding and communications." So this is a combat report of the Pristina Corps Command of 5th June. That's two or three days after the meeting was held. Could you please read 6.1, second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The corps commander and his team are at Djeneral Jankovic in connection with settling issues related to the agreement on the resolution of the Kos Met crisis." I know. I am aware that the commander had visited the village of Djeneral Jankovic, something to do with negotiations leading to that agreement, because I provided security together with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And that was three days after Mr. Sainovic informed you that the -- the agreement was about to be signed and that the police and the army were about to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. One more thing about this visit by General Vasiljevic. At that time, when he was visiting, on your way to the meeting or on your way back, did anyone say it was a meeting of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't speak to General Vasiljevic about the Joint Command at all, nor did he ask me on our way back from the information centre. We didn't discuss it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We'll now move to a different subject. We have to try to move on more quickly and finish before the break. What do you know about the group of volunteers allegedly called "Pauk", Spider?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group of volunteers did not come to the Pristina Corps units bearing that name, "Pauk," Spider. I learned about that group of volunteers when they, on orders of the security administration of the General Staff, were withdrawn from Kosovo and Metohija. As far as I remember, they arrived around the 15th of April, 1999 through regular admissions centres. They were on the regular lists of volunteers, the way volunteers are usually admitted. And they were assigned to units of 125th Motorised Brigade. I believe that was a group of about 30 volunteers. And later, when we sent them away from Kosovo on orders of the security administration of the General Staff, we learned that five of them had left within days. This group was assigned to 125th Motorised Brigade for the simple reason that the chief of security of the 3rd Army asked me which of the subordinate units is suffering the greatest losses, and knowing that the 125th Motorised Brigade had sustained great losses in the area of Kosare border post, where they were constantly under terrorist attack non-stop, and especially badly affected was the 125th Detachment of the military police, I suggested that they be used to replenish and reinforce the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, they were placed in a couple of units within the 125th Motorised Brigade. Where were they engaged?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the general principle of the command that volunteers should not stay as a group, they were individually assigned to various units of the 125th Brigade. And I asked that a few of them be assigned to the 125th Company of the military police, because on a previous occasion some soldiers and the commander of that company were killed and wounded in fighting in Kosare and the company was decimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you know that their name was "Pauk"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did you learn?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned when the chief of the security administration called me. Let me just say that this group was there from the 15th of April until the 5th of May. Just after the 5th of May, the chief called me and asked me, "Do you know that you have a volunteer group somewhere among your units with that name?" I said, "Of course, I don't know. We have no such information." And then the security administration ordered me -- in fact, they sent a fax listing some of the volunteers that they knew as the Spider Group, and he instructed me to find a way urgently to send those people back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When they were sent back, were they tried? Were they prosecuted? And for what?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After they were sent back from Kosovo and Metohija, they were immediately arrested by the MUP, by the police, and charged and prosecuted on charges of preparing an attempt on the life of the president of the country, Mr. Milosevic. The allegation was that they had been infiltrated by foreign countries with a mission to attempt to kill the president, Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any information whether they were responsible for any crimes over the duration of their stay in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That group was only engaged in fighting for two or three days in the area of Kosare border post, and they were not engaged in any other assignment and they did not commit any crimes or offences for the duration of their stay in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My last question about this: What kind of uniforms did they wear while they were engaged in Kosovo those 15 days?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not tour and inspect other members of the group who were not in the military police company, but I did inspect the military police company. It was my duty. And I always saw them wearing the regular uniforms of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We have heard a Prosecution witness here, K73, and in his evidence he stated that part of the 72nd Specialised Brigade was under your command, that they received orders from you to stage attacks on civilians in order to blame them later on the KLA. Are these allegations correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the witness said is a blatant lie. Never, not before and not during the war, did I have command over the 72nd Specialised Brigade or any part thereof or any other special or specialised unit. On orders of the corps commander, I had the obligation to take one battalion of the 72nd Specialised Brigade and drive them to Nasec village in the area of Prizren. That village is on the river-bank of the Beli Drim River. I was to put them up in an abandoned vacation home for children. I later learned that that part of the 72nd Specialised Brigade was assigned to enforce in-depth security in that area, because it's on the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you or any other officer ever order that attacks on civilians be staged, orchestrated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard this allegation before, and it -- it is terribly odd. The military security service of the Pristina Corps had all sorts of information about all sorts of things, but we never ever had any intelligence that would indicate that any member of the army ordered any other members of the army to stage manage an attack on civilians in order to blame that attack on the terrorist organisation of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I have just one more set of questions, brief questions, and not many of them, that has to do with the evidence of another witness, who was not protected, whom we heard before. Did you know Captain First Class Nike Peraj from the 52nd artillery rocket Brigade of the anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we briefly move into private session? I would like to ask a question that might identify somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Identify somebody who needs protection, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I -- I don't know if I should say it in open session. Maybe that itself could point a finger at the person who needs it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll hear the evidence in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we need a break at this stage. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher. That break will be for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, my information from the Detention Unit is that you haven't made a -- a request for a special arrangement to be made tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a strange --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- Information, because we did, really. Mr. Ivetic spoke directly with Mr. Tim McFadden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First we spoke with Maja Marinovic, and she directed us to speak with Mr. McFadden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps something more formal was expected. However, you should now make a formal request and let's see what happens as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that -- I mean now -- by saying "now," I mean now. We shall -- we'll resume at 11.15, since we're going to make as big an effort as we can to complete this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The accused Milutinovic not present].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note that Mr. Milutinovic is unwell and is not in court at this stage but has consented to the continuation of the proceedings in his absence. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, just one sentence. We sent a formal request to the -- to Mr. McFadden to the Detention Unit regarding our visit tomorrow to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. I hope you will get an early reply, and if there remains a problem, let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As we are discussing matters involving Mr. Lukic, I was wondering if I could inquire through the Court whether there is an intention to comply with the Court's order of the 5th of October and when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, that is being dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am specifically dealing with it at the break along with many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is being treated as a matter of urgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, tell me, Captain Nike Peraj, what duty did he have in the unit of the 52nd arbr PVO?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the war, Captain Peraj Nike, in the command of the 52nd artillery rocket Brigade of the anti-aircraft defence performed the duty of assistant commander for the garrison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last word of the reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And was he --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he was one of the desk officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've lost the interpretation at this stage. The last word of your last answer was not picked up. You said that he was assistant commander for the garrison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that Captain Peraj Nike was the assistant commander of the brigade for garrison affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And in the nature of this duty, was he a member of the collegium of the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could he attend collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, Witness Peraj stated here that he attended a meeting between you; the chief of the Djakovica SUP, Kovacevic; the chief of the Djakovica SDB, Cakcamovic [as interpreted]; and a certain man, Major Micunovic, in a house in Djakovica when you allegedly on the occasion of the death of your relative Prascevic said that an action had to be carried out in the Caragoj Valley and that at least 100 people killed and that you would get approved for this from Pavkovic. Is this claim by Witness Peraj correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a completely incorrect allegation. I never attended a single meeting like that. And some of the persons mentioned by Mr. Peraj here are persons whom I do not know. For example, Mr. Kovacevic, as you said; nor did I ever say anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you attend the funeral of your brother-in-law Prascevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not attend the funeral of my brother-in-law Prascevic, but a day before the funeral I went to express my condolences to the family. Mr. Peraj Nike was present at the time. He also came to offer his condolences, and he was a member of the late Prascevic -- a friend - the interpreter's correction - of the late Prascevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you were there to express your condolences to the family, did you say something like that when you were there to condole with the family?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The condolences were being offered in the courtyard of the family house. Mr. Peraj was sitting on a bench with several other people. There were about 100 people present. I approached him, and he also expressed his condolences to me. We didn't talk. We just drank a glass of brandy, and then I had to leave because of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The same witness in his testimony stated that the commander of the Pristina Corps, Lazarevic, in the course of 1999 spent some time in Djakovica and that every day, either in the SUP building or in the building of the Municipal Assembly of Djakovica, meetings were held of the leading people in the army, the MUP, and the municipal authorities, and that at these meetings General Lazarevic was occasionally present. Do you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lazarevic, in the course of 1999, to the best of my recollection, spent time in the Djakovica garrison in early April, when there were major problems concerning the Kosare border post, and there was a major offensive going on by Albanian terrorists from the territory of Albania. To the best of my recollection, there was another time when he spent time in the Djakovica garrison in the course of the war, and that would be in the second half of May. As regards the meetings you mentioned here that were allegedly held in the municipal building, to the best of my knowledge, according to the report by the organ of security of that unit, the 52nd Rocket Brigade, I knew that the brigade commander, as the garrison commander, Colonel Djorsan [phoen], occasionally went to see the chief of the SUP and the president of the municipality in order to regulate certain matters concerning the garrison, and that was part of his job description as garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That hasn't answered your question, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware -- you said that General Lazarevic was in the -- he was in Djakovica on -- only on two occasions, once in April and once in May.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In view of this, could he have attended those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just go back a little, Mr. Bakrac, to page 47, lines 5 and 6. What are the correct names that should be there, the name of the relative and then -- I think it was the Caragoj Valley. So that we get this accurately reflected in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was the question before this, and well, the interpretation was relative. It wasn't relative. It was that Witness Peraj said that this witness, Stojanovic, attended a meeting with the chief of the Djakovica SUP, Kovacevic; the chief of the Djakovica SDB, Camovic; and a certain Major Micunovic in a house in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the occasion of the death of whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the occasion of the death of MUP member Prascevic and that allegedly this witness said that in the Caragoj Valley, because of Prascevic's death, at least 100 people should be killed. The Caragoj Valley, your witness -- Your Honour, is what the witness has already testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in 1999, was the forward command post in Pristina taken up? In Djakovica, excuse me. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Djakovica, up to the beginning of April, I think, the command group was operating. And as of early April, there was a forward command post of the Pristina Corps at which the chief -- Chief of Staff of the corps, Colonel Veroljub Zivkovic was constantly present with a group of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, tell me, let's just take a look at another exhibit. I have two more questions. Let's look at 5D995. General, in item 3 it says -- this is a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on, I'm trying to understand the last answer. And it's perhaps some confusion caused by the question. The question was: Was the forward command post in -- in Djakovica taken up? It possibly was differently expressed in Serbian. I don't know. But your answer is not clear. Can you deal with that again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Djakovica garrison as of March and throughout March, from the beginning of the NATO air-strikes, until early April, there was a command group of the Pristina Corps.
