And then as of the beginning of April, there was a permanent forward command post of the Pristina Corps, headed by the Chief of Staff of the corps, Colonel Veroljub Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, do you know the following persons: Captain Zoran Ristovski, Stefanovic Aleksandar, and Nebojsa Jovanovic, and those two were sergeants first class [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with only two of those, Ristovski and Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Staff sergeant. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were members of the military security service tasked with the airport of Slatina, near Pristina. And professionally and -- they were not subordinated to the security organs of the Pristina Corps but, rather, as regards their military occupational specialty, they were subordinated to the security organs of the command of the air force and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were they arrested in the course of 1999, somewhere in late May?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you can see that from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you personally or your -- or Nesic, in the security organ, exert any pressure on the prosecutor, Djorovic Lakic, to drop the charges against these two?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs of the Pristina Corps and the military police organs never. And - and that include the period of the war - exerted any kind of pressure on the military investigating organs. And in this particular case that you're asking me about specifically, it's not clear why we would exert pressure on the competent judicial organs when it was we, ourselves, who arrested those persons and handed them over to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have only one more question. Let's look at Exhibit 6D142. And I'll tell you right away why I'm showing you this exhibit. Prosecution witness Merovci in his testimony before this Court stated that from the wife of Fehmi Agani he heard that this man had been killed by the army. Do you know anything? And if so, what do you know about the murder of Fehmi Agami?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the document on my screen, but I can answer your question. The Army of the FRY has nothing to do with the murder of Mr. Fehmi Agani, nor did any other organ send to representatives of the army any request to collect information or evidence that might indicate that the army had participated in the murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there seems to be a problem with this exhibit, but we have referred to it and it already has an exhibit number, so we can see from it that the proper procedure was undertaken and a criminal report filed against persons unknown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Bakrac, the exhibit is under seal, but it is there. Can you tell me the number of the previous exhibit that was referred to by the witness, but I have no recollection of a number being called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D995. Your Honour, these were all my questions, unless -- because at the end of yesterday's session, Your Honours asked the witness to try to recall certain officers. Would you like me to probe this further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I have no further questions. But yesterday, at the end of the day, His Honour Judge Bonomy asked you if you can recall any other officers who were prosecuted or any commander.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I did my best to recollect. A lot of time has elapsed, but I will mention a few cases. The following was arrested and prosecuted: Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic from the 37th Motorised Brigade, because he ordered two men from his unit to murder six civilians in the village of Gornja Klina in Srbica municipality. Also, the following was arrested and prosecuted: Captain First Class Dragisa, company commander in the 202nd Rear Base, because in the village of Susica near Pristina he ordered his subordinates, a sergeant and a conscript, to kill two Albanian villagers who were elderly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat this name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of that offender, Captain First Class ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragica Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, Captain First Class Vujadin Stekovic was arrested and prosecuted. He was from the 549th Motorised Brigade. Because in the village of Zagradska Hoca in Prizren municipality, using his own weapon, he killed four Albanian villagers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were any of the -- is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there were more. I can give you some more names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A military disciplinary court saw Vojnova Ratkovic [phoen], the commander of the 7th Detachment of the -- of the -- the 7th Infantry Brigade was brought to court and prosecuted for the looting carried out by members of his unit, and the Chief of Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, the name has not been picked up. What was the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the 7th Detachment of the 7th Infantry Brigade, whose name was Ratkovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Ratkovic. I can't remember his first name. Somebody else who was replaced from duty as Chief of Staff of the 7th Light Infantry Brigade was Lieutenant-Colonel Lazovic, for reasons of desertion -- or rather, because a large -- many members of his unit deserted. And yesterday I said that the other place -- person who was replaced was the commander of the 175th Infantry Brigade, Colonel Petkovic, as well as his Chief of Staff. He was replaced too; Lieutenant-Colonel Zoran Djurasovic was his name. And the chief of the security organ in that place was also replaced. And that was Major Panic, Miroslav Panic. All three men were replaced because they had failed to take the necessary steps and in the area of their responsibility members of their units had perpetrated crimes. They had not taken steps to prevent that. And yesterday I mentioned the example of the arrest of a volunteer, Vlado Zmajevic, along with seven [Realtime transcript read in error "several"] other volunteers for the crimes they had committed in Zegra. And today, I'd like to add to that the following: The arrest of a volunteer by the name of Subotic, who introduced himself as Colonel Subotic, and a group of volunteers from the same brigade who had committed crimes in the village of Prilepnica, Gnjilane municipality. We learnt of their crimes after the corps commander, who was angry because of what had happened in the village of Zegra, had expelled about 40 volunteers from the area, from the territory of Kosovo. And then we, at the level of the security sector of the Pristina Corps Command established -- set up a whole team to take stock of the situation on the ground, and then we received information that that group of volunteers, with Mr. Subotic, had committed crimes in the village of Prilepnica too, the ones I mentioned a moment ago. An order was issued straight away to uncover the -- the volunteers via the security sector of the 3rd Army, and they were all arrested in the Valjevo area and prosecuted. Furthermore --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "in the area of Valjevo," tell us where Valjevo is located. In what territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, it is west of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What I mean is, is Valjevo on the territory of Serbia or in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Kosovo and Metohija is part of Serbian territory too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you for the purposes of these proceedings to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the territory of Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then somebody else who was replaced and prosecuted was a security organ official of the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade, and that was Major Zlatan Mancic, because he had ordered two soldiers to shoot and kill two local villagers in the village of Kusljin in the municipality of Djakovica. Mr. President, there are many others, many other officers who were prosecuted for having failed to take the necessary measures to protect the units. And because of their omissions in exercising command for the crime of theft and for crimes of looting and also for crimes of seizing vehicles belonging to other people. All this information and much more data is to be found in the records of the military courts of the set districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether that is sufficient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, which of your documents reflects this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that during the testimony of General Lazarevic we showed one document, one particular document. I don't know if it contained all this information, but I do know for certain that we did produce the document in the 5D documents, the report of the Pristina Corps Command of the 15th of May, if I remember correctly, informing the units about the measures and steps taken against the officers of the Pristina Corps. And 5D -- the number of the 5D document is -- well, I can provide you with that 5D number a little later on, after I've checked it out, but it is an exhibit. And we also have the testimony of General Gojovic, who testified in the defence of General Ojdanic, who also gave us information about crimes that were prosecuted. And my colleague, Mr. Cepic, will be dealing with the questioning of judges -- or rather, one judge and one prosecutor of the military court attached to the Pristina Corps and the Pristina military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will be all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may be of assistance. One intervention. In transcript 55, 3 and 4, the witness, I believe, said when he was talking about Vlado Zmajevic, a volunteer, he said along with seven other volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He did indeed. That's what I've noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the -- and the crimes that were committed in the village of Zegra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. I understand you have questions, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A general question to start off with. General, the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel, Bakrac, dealt with your knowledge of a possible meeting of the Joint Command in 1999 where General Lazarevic would have to be present, and so on. Now, you were in charge of his security, as far as I understand it, the command of the Pristina Corps, and your people, people subordinate to you, provided security for the command of the Pristina Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We also learnt during the testimony of General Lazarevic that the forward command post of the 3rd Army was in the command post of the Pristina Corps and that General Pavkovic, as commander of the 3rd Army, was present there. Is that right? During the war, of course.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, it was in the area of deployment of the command post of the Pristina Corps, but not physically in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Now, who provided security for General Pavkovic at the time when he was there? Who was the security detail in the region where General Lazarevic was too? Who was responsible for his security? You or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules and regulations that were in force regulating security for high-level military personnages state that if any high-ranking military leader from the superior command was in the area of responsibility of a lower command, then responsibility for his security was borne by the command on whose territory the person was located, and therefore it was my duty during General Pavkovic's stay - of course, in addition to one or two security details - to provide security for General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please. Would the speakers kindly slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, if General Pavkovic were to attend those meet, for instance, in addition to General Lazarevic -- and you've explained that to us already - would you have to provide security or your people would have to provide security for him too, or not? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly if there were meetings of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is logical to assume that General Lazarevic would not have a meeting with himself, nor would General Pavkovic have a meeting with himself. Then in this Joint Command they would have had to have met with someone else, apart from themselves. Now, by virtue of the Prosecution's position and in the indictment, those people who were -- those peoples that would have meetings would be Nikola Sainovic and at least three to four policemen: General Sreten Lukic, Rodja Djordjevic, Obrad Stevanovic, or somebody like that. So that would be a serious set of people. Now, how would you provide security for them to be there together to support the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly if a meeting of that level with such distinguished people were to be held, then, of course, I, as the chief of security of the military police would have certain responsibilities and authority in the sense of providing broader security for the area and more detailed forms of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would there be police security and would there be security for Nikola Sainovic too? Would they be present too, the security details for them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I'm sure that their security -- that it was the MUP who were in charge of their security on the basis of the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's clear now. I won't ask you about that. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, are you saying that there was no point in time when General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic would be together in the one building or place at the centre of both their command posts; that they were physically -- always physically in separate places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the forward command post of the 3rd Army, and the command post of the Pristina Corps were not in the same location. And according to the rules, they cannot be in the same location. However, the command of the 3rd Army, General Pavkovic, and the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic, could physically be at the same place together, but on the basis of the regulations you can't have the commander of one and the same unit and his Chief of Staff. They can't be physically in the same place or transported physically in the same vehicle, because if anything were to happen to them, the command wouldn't be able to function without them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's go back for a moment to the 1st of June meeting, 1st of June, 1999. And I want to ask you first, General: When you described those present, of the police force you just mentioned General Sreten Lukic. So I'd ask you ask you now whether Obrad -- or rather, Stevanovic and Obrad Djordjevic may have been present as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, I'm quite sure about the persons that I said attended. I'm sure about those. But possibly there was another MUP representative, but I'm quite certain that General Djordjevic was not present or the other man you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General. Now I'm going to ask you briefly about something else, not to use up our valuable court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I'm sorry about that again, but two names you gave just now were -- I'm confused now. Now, I'm sure Djordjevic's first name is not Obrad. We've got Obrad Stevanovic now but --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Obrad Stevanovic and General Vlastimir Djordjevic is his proper name. Rodja is a nickname. So Vlastimir is his first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm going to go through these questions very quickly. Just "yes" or "no" answers, please. The meetings that you attended, was it a meeting of the Joint Command at all, in your opinion, knowledge, awareness, or anything else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you gain the impression that at that meeting a report was being tabled or that any orders were being issued at all? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not gain that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, in a word, would you tell me the following -- or in a sentence, because you can't say "yes" or "no." How did you understand the reason for Sainovic's attendance at that meeting? Why was he there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I share the opinion of all those present. At the meeting I understood the presence of Mr. Sainovic at that meeting as his presence there in his capacity of a high-ranking state official who had come to inform us that there would be the signing of an agreement in the future. And that was the condition for NATO to stop its bombing and that the army and MUP would be withdrawing from Kosovo on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Sainovic, did he issue any orders to anyone at that meeting, any type of order whatsoever? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please. I've said a number of times. The meeting lasted for just 10 to 15 minutes, and nobody issued anybody else any order whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We're now going to deal with Vasiljevic's testimony, who was heard in this court of law, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic testified here. And he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- Mr. Fila. Just to be clear about this, the impression you gave earlier in your evidence was that Mr. Sainovic and Andjelkovic came in and just sat down as if that was routine. Would it be wrong to get that impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Your impression is wrong. When we were sitting down, they came into the room afterwards. And out of respect, we got to our feet. We stood up. And then there was a short briefing of 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well your answer earlier was, "When we were sitting -- when we were sitting down, Mr. Sainovic came in and Mr. Andjelkovic and they sat down at the same table as General Pavkovic and Lazarevic. We were sitting next to them." And the whole impression of that answer was this is just a routine arrival. But you say not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's a standard behaviour in the army that when somebody senior comes in, out of respect, out of good manners -- they sat in front of us. Everyone else was sitting down. But we got up when they came in. It was a round table. Nobody wrote anything down. They just listened to what was being said. I don't really know what else I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anybody chair that meeting? Did Sainovic chair it, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody was the chairman. I just said that General Pavkovic introduced Mr. Sainovic, saying he had come to inform us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you left the meeting, you and General Vasiljevic. So you didn't stay for dinner. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any dinner after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Earlier on, responding to a question from the Bench and from Defence counsel, you said that General Vasiljevic stayed for a few days on his visit to Kosovo and Metohija. At any point during his visit did you speak, did you tell General Vasiljevic anything about a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I will now read to you exactly what General Vasiljevic said in his evidence. If somebody is very curious, I'll give a reference. So Vasiljevic says that he received information from you. Page 8802. When you were going back from that meeting at the Pristina Corps -- you said you never went to the Pristina Corps at all. Anyway, on your way to the building where security offices were - that's Exhibit P2594, paragraph 83 - to the effect that the Joint Command is a mini Supreme Command in Kosovo and Metohija that, it's a dislocated command post - Exhibit 2594, paragraph 7 - that the Joint Command was set up in 1998; that General Dimitrijevic asked from you that you should report on the work of that command, because there was no need for you to participate in it, since high-ranking officials from Belgrade were present, Minic, Matkovic, Sainovic - P2594, paragraph 84 - any of these things I've just said? Is anything correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything you've said is completely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'll ask you something else now. That 10 to 15-minute meeting that you spoke about, did anybody keep notes? Did anybody make a record?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. Nobody kept minutes or a record. Nobody even took notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did General Vasiljevic note anything down in a notepad or a notebook that you could see?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, but it seems to me that neither he or I had a notebook or a notebook -- notepad. I don't recall that anybody opened any kind of notepad or notebook or took any notes at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, in his interview to the OTP on the 22nd November 2001, Exhibit 6D158, page 33 - in the English version, it's page 43 - I can call it up on the screen, and perhaps it's even better for you to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That number is accurate, 6D158?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6D158. Page 33 in B/C/S -- in Serbian, rather; and 43 in English. Could we zoom in. I can give you a hard copy, but still we need to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This passage begins -- read from line 20 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you please read from the words "I did not." Do you see it? Somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Mr. Fila, what your purpose is in referring to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the purpose is that General Vasiljevic says here that he had not even taken a notebook with him and he didn't have it there. The purpose is to establish what General Vasiljevic said in his interview, and then I'll come to what he testified before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But did you put this to General Vasiljevic as contradicting his evidence? I doubt it, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ivetic did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because that's when the notebook appeared. Why should I show it when Ivetic was doing that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am keeping --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As long as someone has done it, that's enough. But my information is that this document has not been exhibited. And this is the first -- this is its first introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I announced it to the Prosecution and said that I will tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not part of the case at the moment. And are you -- are you -- are you seriously intending to -- to introduce it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This passage, I want to use. Only that passage. Only that one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that can very well lead to extensive other parts of it being used by the Prosecution. But if you're happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him use whatever. It is of no consequence to me what the Prosecutor will use. I never objected to anything of the sort, because I'm sure that what is there is what I think and cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's an issue -- there's an issue here that we have to resolve. I'm -- I'm not understanding at the moment what it is you're trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am trying to have read a part of the exhibit used by Mr. Ivetic. In that sentence, it reads that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He did not use that exhibit, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He put it in the system and gave it the number 6D158. Now I want to use that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For what --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm seeking leave to -- to show that in the interview he said what is written there and in the next piece of evidence, you will see what that same man, Vasiljevic, said sitting before you. I want to establish which of the two is true. Because there is a difference between what he said in the interview and what he said sitting before you, in his testimony, and, again, what this witness is saying. And General Vasiljevic is a very important witness for 1999, and it's very important to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp, your submissions on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that Mr. Fila has indicated what he proposes to do with that document, this is not something for this witness to comment upon. The witness has said quite -- has said more than once, "I cannot recall if anyone had any notebook or if -- or took notes." And therefore if there is something that Vasiljevic might have said in one place or in another place, then this witness is not in a position to comment on that, having regard to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness can tell us what exactly happened. The witness, Your Honours, will tell us what really happened according to him. And I'm showing him what General Vasiljevic said and that pertains directly to this witness. And after testifying before you, after Vasiljevic testifying before you, this workbook, this notebook appeared, and it became a piece of evidence. That's why it's important, because we don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's enough, I think. We don't want to undermine the witness's evidence by discussing what -- what you may be about to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we do not consider that presenting this statement to the witness is the way to go about this exercise. This is not something that's part of the evidence in this case at this moment. It may yet become part of the evidence in some way or other, but it can't be introduced as evidence through the questions you're asking this witness. On the other hand, you can put the meat of what's in the statement, the -- the propositions that are in the statement, and ask the witness whether he agrees or disagrees with them. But they should not be put as specific quotations from Vasiljevic in an interview that he had with the Office of the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Even that will be quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, then, you see, I told you General Vasiljevic first said he did not have a notebook, that he didn't keep notes, and you confirmed that. Is that consistent with your recollection? That's how it happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this appropriate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you've been listening into the evidence in the case. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I asked only about notes. Is that consistent with his recollection that on that occasion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is what you mustn't do, Mr. Fila. If there's something in there, you -- it's not appropriate to attribute it to Vasiljevic in putting your question. You can put the hypothetical position that if something was said, is that consistent with your recollection of what actually happened on the occasion? Just get to the heart of the matter. You're -- you're actually using this as a speech, as a submission, and that's not appropriate either. This witness is here to give us his recollection, not to comment on -- on any discrepancies there may be between different versions given by Vasiljevic or whether the versions are -- are consistent with each other, or whatever. That's not his job. His job is to tell us what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, his job is to answer what he remembers, and I'm asking him does he remember that General Vasiljevic took notes or not on the occasion when they were at a meeting together? That's quite simple. That's what I asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he take notes or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither General Vasiljevic or anyone else kept any notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, let's make an assumption. If - if - General Vasiljevic were to hand over a notebook to us with some notes in it that he allegedly had taken on that occasion, would that be true or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are rules in the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that govern treatment of documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please -- please listen to the question. You're not answering the question you've been asked. It's a matter of fact you're being asked about. Whether it breaks the rules or is consistent with the rules is neither here nor there. Just tell us if whether General Vasiljevic handed over a notebook here, could that possibly be notes taken on the occasion of that meeting. I know it's a silly question, because you've already answered it, but never mind. You're being asked it. So please try and answer. In fact, what we should do, since there's confusion here. Mr. -- Mr. Fila, that question -- the answer to that question adds nothing to what you've already heard from the witness. So let's go to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll move on. I would like Exhibit 2D391 to be shown. We did not see it before. It's a letter from the government of Serbia to the National Committee, I believe. And it's written there -- Page 1, please. In fact, page 2. Page 2, and then I'll tell you briefly -- it's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You will see it says in one passage that General Djakovic had turned in his notebook from the said period; whereas, General Vasiljevic did not. I would like to know: Is there an obligation on the part of army officers to turn in their workbooks once they are completed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the duty of every professional member of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to register duly every service notebook in the register, and once a notebook is used up, he has to turn it in, in order to be issued with another. Service notebooks constitute official documents and correspondence according to the Rules of Yugoslavia and the Rules of Treatment of Documentation prescribed for how long they are kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If that had been done, then we would have been able to obtain a copy of that blue notebook. We would know that it is the real one and how it was kept, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We note that the exhibit that's just been referred to has not previously been exhibited in the case and that the witness has no knowledge of the contents. He was simply telling us what the rules in relation to notebooks are.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I used it, only so that he could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. My name is Tomislav Visnjic, and I appear for General Ojdanic here. I'll put a few questions to you. During your examination-in-chief, you mentioned inter alia when enumerating the organs active on the territory of Kosovo in 1998 and 1998 [as interpreted] counter-intelligence groups. General, am I correct in saying that the domain that these counter-intelligence groups dealt with was the protection of the Army of Yugoslavia from external threats to the security of the units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in a manner of speaking. But could you allow me to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence groups are expert teams composed of organs of the military security service, and their main purpose is to monitor the influence of the security situation on the territory on the security of army personnel and facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So these were not organs whose main task was to detect, discover, and prosecute persons suspected of crimes which are relevant for this Tribunal, crimes against humanity, the laws of war, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 3D721, page 2 in both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we have before us a document which are minutes from the evening briefing in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and we won't dwell on it for long. I'm only interested in one line in this document. And in order to avoid going back to the previous page, it begins with General Gajic's taking the floor. And what I'm interested in is in the middle of this text, where he says: "A group of 32 volunteers was sent back from Kosovo and Metohija (seven looted)," and so on. General, this is a piece of information which was discussed at the evening briefing in the Supreme Command Staff. Is this information you are aware of and was it sent by the corps up the chain of command? The date is the 3rd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this piece of information refers to something I've just mentioned, concerning the problem of volunteers in the area of Gnjilane and Zegra.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I don't need the details. I just wanted to confirm that this information was sent on by the corps, that it was forwarded by the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 3D589, page 1 in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is another evening briefing in the Supreme Command Staff, dated the 18th of April, 1999. And in item 1, the last three lines -- or in item 2 it says: "I draw attention -- I would like to mention the drastic case." That's in item 2, last paragraph -- "from the 52nd arbr PVO, regarding rape and looting," and so on. And my question is the same as in the previous case. Is this information that you are aware of and was it forwarded up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These persons were prosecuted. This was a crime committed in the village of Crnjani in the municipal assembly of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, several witnesses testified about something I would like to confirm with you now. Is it correct that every combat report contains a special section, a separate section concerning security? We have witnesses who even said that this was usually item 5 of a combat report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the item number was in the combat report, the one dealing with security, but I know that every combat report did contain a section about security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the security organ participated in this by delivering information or drawing up the content, the text; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now move on to a new topic. General, did you ever report -- when I say "you," I mean your organ or the corps command - the following: Acting independently on the ground, a member -- a number of members of the MUP and entire small units are perpetrating grievous crimes against the Siptar civilian population in villages or in refugee camps: Murders, rapes, looting, robbery, aggravated theft, and so on, and they are deliberately ascribing these crimes or preparing to ascribe them to units and individuals from the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anything to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 3D493.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we are moving on now to another topic. This is the evening briefing in the Supreme Command Staff of the 8th of June, 1999. And it's what General Geza Farkas said. I think that in e-court we have a printed version of the same document, and it might be easier for the witness to see the typed-out version. Thank you. Could we turn to page 2 in B/C/S. Thank you. And also page 2 in English. General, you testified about the inspections which the security organs of the General Staff conducted in the course of the war operations and war activities. And this is a report -- or rather, it's what General Farkas said at the briefing on the return of the second inspection -- the completion of the second inspection by General Vasiljevic and General Gajic. I'll start with the part where he says: "There are problems, humanitarian crime, an analysis -- a complete analysis has been carried out under the leadership of the deputy chief of the security administration. Most of the crimes have been documented and are before the military judicial organs. There are serious crimes ranging from looting or robbery to rape. There are all sorts of things. How far have they got with the investigations if 95 per cent have been arrested and are under investigation. There are some from our active units." I would like to stop here. And my question, General, is the following: Is this a summary of Generals -- of what Generals Gajic and Vasiljevic established when visiting your units? And I am especially referring to the very high percentage of crimes that had been processed.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. This is the gist of what they observed during their tour, and they also mentioned the number I mentioned, of 95 per cent of those prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's now move on to another topic. When testifying about a certain meeting which was held in Hotel Grand, you said that the meeting was attended also by General Kovacevic. I can't find the reference now, but it's in today's record. You said that he was late for the meeting. As far as I could understand, you said that the meeting lasted 10 to 15 minutes. General, do you allow for the possibility that General Kovacevic turned up after the meeting was already over and that you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came midway through the meeting. He was late for the beginning. He had been on the ground, and he came back halfway through the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, as far as I could understand, you do not have a notebook and you are testifying relying on your memory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. For this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: First I would like to ask you something about today's transcript which is still not clear. On page 38, lines 14 to 18, when answering to a question put by Mr. Bakrac about the "Pauk" or Spider Group, and you said: "After the 1st of May I was called by the chief and then soon after that I received a fax with the names of those persons". Could you just clarify: Who called you up on the phone and from whom you received this fax.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the security administration called me up. As for the fax, I don't know who from the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Where did you get the fax from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yesterday during the examination-in-chief by my colleague Mr. Bakrac, and also today, you said that the Military Police Battalion of the Pristina Corps in the professional line of duty was subordinated to you. I would like to ask you whether you are aware that General Pavkovic before the war, before the war started, held a speech to the members of the Military Police Battalion of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Pavkovic addressed -- well, he visited almost all the units, including the 52nd Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I need some guidance. I would like to show the witness a video-clip, a brief one, but it's under seal, because it was shown to a protected witness. I don't know whether we should move into private session briefly, or maybe we can do that after the break. Whatever Your Honours decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it show something that needs to be protected?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed with the video-clip, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I think it does. I think it -- if I -- you see, I don't know where my friend is going with it. But if it is the same clip I am thinking of, he may be asking him to identify someone who might be protected. I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I won't be asking that. No, I won't put that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it sounds as though there's uncertainty, so let's have it in private session. 10 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's 4D18, and we have a transcript of General Pavkovic's speech accompanying the image, all in the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It looks as though you're going to have to proceed without it, Mr. Aleksic. Can you ask your question without the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. But may what is on my screen be zoomed into. I can't see it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There shouldn't be anything on your screen. Well, we'll adjourn just now and have a break. But you need to think whether it's necessary to show videos like this to establish anything in particular. We'll see that after lunchtime, when hopefully there will be no technical glitches. Again, please, Mr. Stojanovic, could you leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you again at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in -- no. In fact, I'll deal with it later when we're in open session. At the moment, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't think there are any more technical glitches, so perhaps we could see the next exhibit. 4D18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please -- please stop it. Are you wanting us to hear what's being said? Because you did refer to a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. The transcript is attached to what General Pavkovic says in English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope, then, that the interpreters will translate this as he speaks. So let's go back and start it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem for all of us is we can't see the transcript, and it's the same for the interpreters, without hard copy. So how do you propose dealing with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the B/C/S in hard copy, so perhaps we could put it on the ELMO and facilitate the interpreters that way. Otherwise, technically I don't know how we can do this. I understand that we can't see the image and for you to hear what General Pavkovic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, I can actually get it on the other screen here. Is that not possible for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can get it on the screen, so we can now view it without the -- we don't need the interpretation. We can read it on the other screen as it goes, so please continue with the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just make the observation that we have no information as to the provenance or -- well, it seems to be a record, but we don't know where this is from. And I make the observation because on the last time a video was played, it was played and then the witness was told where it came from and what it's all about. So I'd ask that if we're going to go through the same procedure, then the witness, not counsel, be able to testify about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You take that point, Mr. Aleksic, that once you've shown it, you should ask the witness what he can tell us to identify what this is, rather than put to him what you say it is. Okay? So proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Well, as far as terrorism is concerned, that is, terrorist forces, we must deal with them very quickly and efficiently, and there's no dilemma there. And then if we do have such a strong opponent, then let him remain alone. However, we have to bear in mind here that all other local traitors have to be dealt with, those who have lately been arguing that we cannot oppose the entire world and that we cannot fight against the entire world. I don't know who it is that we are preparing to fight against, who this whole world is. We are only preparing to defend our country, regardless of the opponent who attacks it. Others are trying to argue that certain Generals are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop it. There's no need for us to go through all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognize this footage and were you present on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognize the footage, the video. It was taken in the barracks -- the Kosovski Junaci barracks in Pristina, just prior to the NATO aggression, when the commander of the army, the commander of 3rd Army, that is, General Pavkovic, and the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic, attended an exercise performed by members of the 52nd Battalion of the military police on the training ground which was close by. And you can see it on this footage. And afterwards, General Pavkovic informed the composition of the 52nd Military Police Battalion, after the exercise and training had been completed, he reported to -- informed them. And I was present there too, although I can't see myself on the picture. But he informed them about the current situation just before the NATO bombing started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you tell us, to the best of your recollections, whether that was the only time that General Pavkovic addressed the members of the Military Police Battalion from the beginning of 1999, when he took over that duty as commander of the 3rd Army and up to the war.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only time he addressed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd now like to move on to another area. Yesterday, during Mr. Bakrac's examination, and today again, when Mr. Visnjic asked you, you talked about the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group. And yesterday you said, in response to a question from Mr. Bakrac, on page 57, that the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you now tell me why that was in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said there was no need, and then my learned friend Mr. Stamp said we might run a risk, and then you said that since we weren't sure and there were some doubts, we'd go ahead with it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, why were we in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last time, I think, the Defence of Pavkovic used this video with a witness or attempted to use this video, I think, they wanted the witness to identify somebody on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that person would have been a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then we order that the private session that we've just -- has just concluded will be made public, and we'll now return to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I will repeat that. The private session we've just had that will be made public. Mr. Aleksic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, let me repeat my question. Yesterday and today you said something about the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group, and yesterday you told Mr. Bakrac when he asked you that the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group was directly subordinated to the security sector of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Does it emerge from that that the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group was duty-bound to report back directly to its superior command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now on e-court may we have Exhibit 3D246, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, when the document comes up on our screens, take a look at it and tell us if you recognize it; and if so, can you give us your comments on paragraph 3, please. 3D246, please. It's not the right document. 1046, not 246. 1046, please. Shall we zoom in, General?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who is sending this, who it is addressed to, and to give us your comments on paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a telegram of the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group from the group, addressed to the security administration of the General Staff, to the security organ of the 3rd Army, and to the security organ of the Pristina Corps. And paragraph 3 deals with the following. It says that: "A terrorist group from the area of Drenica ordered all the Albanians from the village of Brusnik, Vucitrn municipality, to leave the village because in the coming days they plan to conduct combat operations there."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, General. As the security organ in the corps, were you aware of this information, this report, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We exchanged -- we did exchange information with the security organs of the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group, and I did know about them on the basis of this kind of information that was sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we may have on e-court Exhibit 4D511. 511.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for the document to appear on our screens, General, once again, I'd like to ask you -- the number of the exhibit again is 4D511. I don't think we have the right English translation on the screen. That's fine now. General, may we have your comments, please, on this document. Just looking at the first two paragraphs. I'm interested in the first two paragraphs and your knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is information from the security organ of the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group, and it relates to the fact that in certain settlements of Kosovska Mitrovica there were several thousand refugees and that amongst those refugees there were several hundred members of the Kosovo Liberation Army. That means that they had camouflaged themselves. Well, we knew about this from other pieces of information that after launching terrorist activities, they used the population to mask themselves or to join the refugees and mask themselves that way so as to prevent them coming into contact with the security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what paragraph you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It says: "In the territory of Vucitrn municipality." That paragraph. Did you receive the information contained in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this was sent to the security organ of the Pristina Corps, as we can see, and I did indeed receive this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the date when this document was issued? Can we see the date? Can you zoom out so we can see the whole document? The B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- this document is dated the 15th of April, 1999. And in view of the location of the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group, I received it the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now on e-court, please, the next document P -- 5D1310. 5D1310, which was used yesterday -- or, rather, mentioned yesterday by my learned friend, Mr. Bakrac, but he didn't dwell on it. He just mentioned it in passing and it is linked to 5D1311.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Would you please just comment on item 1, which is on page 1, and paragraph 5, which is on page 2 of both the B/C/S and English versions.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document refers to another document by which the security section of the command of the 3rd Army is informing the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff about the results of information interviews with terrorists Aslan Sopi and another terrorist who had been captured. If you return the first page, I'll know who they are, their names. And also, of the results of the operative activity of the security organ and the consequences to the units of NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, is this information -- or rather, this report, is it based on information delivered by you to the security organ of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of this information relates to information I sent to the security section of the 3rd Army and the part concerning the results of the information interviews with the two terrorists who had been arrested is information which the security organs of the 3rd Army obtained themselves in those interviews. After the arrest of those two, I handed them over, together with a criminal report, to the security organ of the 3rd Army, the security section, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And with reference to item 5, did you have this information? Did you know about this event? And was it you who reported about this to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday I spoke about the problems faced by the security organs and the military police of the Pristina Corps in implementing their prescribed duties. This item speaks of the escorting of two conscripts from the Prizren Military Territorial Detachment to the Prizren detention, where the military court had its seat, and these two conscripts and members of the military police escorting them were kidnapped and their fate is unknown to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have in e-court Exhibit 4D512. Let's look at page 1 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on who is sending this document, to whom.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document sent by the security department of the 3rd Army command. It's addressed to the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff, and it refers to information --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: What's the date, General, please? Can you tell us the date?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 2nd of May, 1995 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there's a misinterpretation. 89, line 10, it's May 1999, not 1995. In the original, one can see it's the 2nd of May, the fifth month of 1999. Could we see page 2 in both English and B/C/S. I'm interested in item 8, General. If you can take a look and tell us whether you had information to this effect?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Item 8 refers to some information that in Dren village, Zubin Potok municipality, there was a massacre of civilians. We verified this, we checked it, and sent a written report saying that we had not found any information or any traces of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at item 12. It's on the last page in B/C/S and on page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you to ask me to comment on item 12. It refers to the results of the work of the security organs of the army military police of the 3rd Army. The number of criminal reports filed, and categories of persons who had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court 4D513, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I would like to know who sent this, to whom, and when. And if you can comment on item 1. I think you've already referred to this, but I would like you to confirm this information.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the security organ of the 3rd Army, addressed, again, to the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff. And item 1 refers to something we've already mentioned here more than once. It's the inadmissible conduct of certain individual soldiers from the 52nd Artillery Brigade of the anti-aircraft defence in the Djakovica municipality who were dealt with. They were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: What was the crime?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. There's one more point I'd like to ask you about. There's no need to go into private session. But Witness K73 testified before this Tribunal. I don't have the exact page reference, but I don't think this will be in dispute. And this witness said that General Pavkovic, when addressing the members of the Military Police Battalion of the Pristina Corps, said more or less the following: That when the first NATO bomb landed, the soldiers of the Army of Yugoslavia had to get the Albanians off their backs. And in a statement which is in evidence, K73 said that he thought this referred to Albanian civilians. In view of the post you held, do you know whether General Pavkovic ever said anything like that to anyone -- anybody?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said just a while ago that I attended a meeting in the Kosovski Junaci barracks and that neither then nor on any other occasion did I hear General Pavkovic give any such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. My name is Branko Lukic. I appear for the Defence of General Sreten Lukic before this Tribunal today. You gave us a broad picture, which is quite normal, in view of the tasks you performed. I will have only a few questions for you, pinpointing the police and the information you had at that period of time. First, I wish to ask you: Did you know of the existence of formations under the abbreviated name of OPG, operative -- did you know about these OPGs in Kosovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this when General Vasiljevic, whom we have already mentioned, was there. And he said that at the Djakovica SUP there was some sort of operative search group, or something like that, OPG, and he said that he had heard of this from Captain Perovic. A pursuit or search group. I knew of the existence of intervention units in 1998, which were to intervene if a MUP check-point on a road was attacked. I didn't know about the existence of any other groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time that they were part of the PJP units within the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of a crime that happened in Podujevo when a group was brought there by buses?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that this group which committed that crime were the SAG [as interpreted] reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. But if you want me to explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, all I wanted to know was whether you knew they were SAJ reserves?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the perpetrators were prosecuted and sentenced, convicted?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the first to obtain such information personally. They were prosecuted and tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I wish to ask you about the parapolice formations in Kosovo and Metohija. Various witnesses in this trial mentioned different formations which in 1999 were in Kosovo and Metohija. Some of these formations were described as paramilitary or parapolice units by witnesses. So I would like to ask you about some of these. Are you aware that in Kosovo and Metohija there were parapolice or paramilitary units called the Wolves of the Drina [Realtime transcript read in error "Wolves of Drenica], led by Nedeljko Karisik? Also known as "Legenda," who was the former commander of a special MUP unit, and that they were stationed in Kosovo Polje? Was anything like that disclosed to you in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such unit on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In view of the job I did, I'm sure I would have known about it, had there been such a unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a transcript correction. It should be Wolves of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Not Wolves of Drenica but Wolves of Drina. Another correction, Your Honour. My question was that this commander of special MUP unit of -- of Republika Srpska. So it's from Bosnia-Herzegovina, not MUP of Republic of Serbia. But I think that the witness answered. If you want me to clarify it further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in the course of your work, did you obtain information that in Kosovo and Metohija there was active a parapolice formation called Arkan's Tigers and that they were located in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you have not heard of that, I assume we may conclude that you never obtained information that Goran Radosavljevic, "Gurij," was in commander of that unit, Arkan's Tigers. There was a witness who said that, so I have to ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosovo Polje, to the best of my knowledge, there was no such unit. And Goran Radosavljevic, "Gurij," as far as I know, was one of the clerks in the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is the following: Did you obtain information that in Djakovica there was a group called Legija commanded by Colonel Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the information I had. But when I visited General -- or rather, when General Vasiljevic visited the units of the Pristina Corps - and I accompanied him personally - in the Djakovica garrison the chief of the 52nd Artillery Brigade of the PVO, Sergej Perovic, Captain First Class, reported to him and said that there was some such group, but he didn't say who was in command of that group. At that meeting, he was given the task by General Vasiljevic of checking whether any such unit existed and to report to me. After a few days, because Major Perovic then said that this was unverified information -- after a few days, he reported to me that he had not obtained any information indicating the existence of such a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So when something is reported on the basis of data that has not been checked out, then you have to investigate it, right, and check it out?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always and at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know someone called Milan Jolovic, nicknamed "Legija," from the 52nd Special Brigade, which up to the first six months of that same year was the commander of the Special Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That completes what I had to ask you about the paramilitary units. Now I have a few questions -- well, I'd like to pick your brains and talk about the authorisations of the security organs compared to authorised services and persons from the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. You commented on Article 30 of the law governing the army and the powers that officials had from the security organs, and you said that they were identical, of course, in relation to the army, as were the powers and authorities of officials of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the officials of the security organs and of the military police base their work, in addition to the Law Governing the Army, also on the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the same Law on Criminal Procedure which the members of the MUP rely on for their powers and authorisations; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that that is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, General, that authorised personnel of the security organs and of the military police can take into custody military or other persons whom they come across engaged in crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say "military personnel"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Military personnel or civilians or members of the MUP or SUP, to take into custody, if they belong to the army, and to arrest civilians and hand them over to the MUP, if they are civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this. If a member of the Army of Yugoslavia is caught in the act of committing a crime or they come across the perpetrators of critical -- of crimes for military protection -- doing acts against military protection, then they are duty-bound to take them into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about civilians or a policeman engaged in a criminal act? What are they powers and duties there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are duty-bound to inform the superior officer about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you something now about uniforms, the uniforms of certain categories or branches of the army. Can you tell us what kind of uniforms the members of the military police wore? What caps they had on their heads, what colour they were, and what side-arms they had, and any other equipment they possessed.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the military police had one of several types of prescribed uniforms in the Army of Yugoslavia, and they were the M93-type uniform, and they had black berets on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And side-arms and equipment? When I say "equipment," did they have -- carry handcuffs, batons, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the necessary equipment on them that they needed to take anybody into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what uniforms the members of the 72nd Special Brigade wore. Caps, weapons, and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the 72nd Special Brigade also wore the M93-type uniform, but they had red berets on their heads and they had none of the other equipment that other people had to take persons into custody when the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the 63 -- 63rd Parachute Unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the 63rd Parachute Unit also had the M93-type uniform, with a red beret on their heads, but with the visible sign and insignia denoting their -- them as being members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us today on page 17, line 2 about the army check-points in order to control the entrance and exit of soldiers from the area. But do you know that at the critical time there were mixed check-points set up by the army and the police? And if you knew about them, tell us what their purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
