utterances.text: Yes, I do know about the fact that there were mixed check-points manned by the police and the army jointly, pursuant to order from the corps commander of the 4th of April, 1999; however, only a set number of mixed check-points along the main roads and approach roads to certain towns, such as Pristina, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you mentioned something, but I have to ask you about it again. The military districts, did they have units of the military police? And to whom were they responsible, if they did?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military districts, regions, or sectors. The military sectors did not have police units, but the military districts did have units of the military police of platoon level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And they were responsible to whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the commander of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard when the military courts were established. Now, do you know when they actually started functioning? When did you first hear of a military investigating judge going out on a location, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military courts attached to the Pristina Corps Command and attached to the command of the military district of Pristina started functioning on the 26th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So they became functional on the same day they were established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were established several days before that, but they actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Thank you for that answer. They were established on the 24th. Now, you were asked today something about the killing of Fehmi Agani. I don't know why the document wasn't shown you. I don't know that we asked that the document should be under seal, but I'll ask you without the document: Do you know, during the course of your work, did you learn or receive information that the proceedings linked to investigating who had -- who committed the murder was done by the investigating judge, that is, the judge in charge of the investigation, the prosecutor, and the police, pursuant to the law? Do you have any knowledge about any of that? Was everything done according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, by the book?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, everything was done by the book or according to the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's all my team had. These are all the questions we had to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Stojanovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Stamp for the Prosecutor. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me ask you first, do you know of any reasons, any concrete reasons, why Witness Nike Peraj would tell -- would make statements about you that are untrue? And if you want to go into private session to answer, you could ask.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need. I'm not going to mention any names. But I will say that the reasons -- well, as far as I know, he made several statements to this Court and they were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the reasons for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about different statements. I'm asking you simply: Do you know of any concrete reason why he would state matters about you that were not true?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the person whose name is contained in your question, I was friends for many years. There's not a single reason except to say that after he remained living where he was, the KLA blackmailed him into giving false statements. He was afraid for his family and himself, because until the end of the war, he was an active member of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know of any concrete reason why General Vasiljevic would make untrue statements about you when he said that you told him about the Joint Command meeting on the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no reason. And in my statement and testimony, I told the truth. Otherwise, if you're interested, my relations with General Vasiljevic are very proper and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You -- you would have -- well, you did say that you participated in the collegium meetings of the Pristina Corps on a daily basis. Would you, in your capacity as chief of security for the corps, participate in the preparation of plans for combat or tactical manoeuvres of the various units of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would take part in the work of the command in making decisions commensurate to my powers and authorities as chief of the security organ of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would ask you to listen to the questions. You know, did you hear the last question I asked you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'd like you to answer it this time: Did you participate in the preparation of plans for combat actions or manoeuvres of the various units of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in the part which related to giving over information and providing knowledge about the locations, plans, intentions, strength of the Albanian terrorists, and that information I sent to the chief of the department for operations of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you participate in that capacity in the planning and preparation of the army deployment in Meja on the 26th, 27th, and 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did your unit provide any information for the preparation of the plans for that army operation on those dates?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs constantly provided information on the presence of terrorists in all localities throughout Kosovo and Metohija, including the presence of terrorists in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you know that there was a major combined army-MUP offensive down the Caragoj Valley to Meja and Korenica on the 26th, 27th, and 28th of April, 1999? Do you know that there was such an exercise?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for that exercise, I learnt about it later, not in whole but on a need-to-know basis, as prescribed by my position. And in each unit, I have a security organ who has his responsibility and function vis-a-vis the units. And if you're mentioning the units in the action in Caragoj Valley, then each unit had its own security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long after that operation did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The competent security organs were duty-bound after every operation to report to me, as the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking about a specific operation, the operation in Meja and the Caragoj Valley of 27th and 28th of April, 1999. When did you find out about it? What date?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about it in the evening hours through the report from the chief of security of the 52nd Artillery Battalion of air defence, Captain First Class Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the evening hours of the 27th or 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think it was the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Weren't military police units, in particular the 52nd -- all right. I'll give you the precise -- the 52nd Battalion of the military police involved as participants in that operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that operation, to the best of my knowledge, two platoons of the military police took part from the 52nd Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you not informed about an operation, a major operation, in the neighbourhood that you came from at any of the collegium meetings that you said you attended on a daily basis? Did you hear about this being planned at any collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when the operation took place, I myself was elsewhere. I can't remember which location now. And I do believe that the corps commander was certainly on some other assignment; so that we did not hold a collegium at that time. At the forward command post, as I said, you had the Chief of Staff of the corps, and he was Colonel Veroljub Zivkovic, who was responsible for all activities of the units in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you know where General Lazarevic was on the 27th of April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lazarevic on the 27th of April was in the Pristina garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know where he was on the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of April, he was also at the Pristina garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of him visiting any units on any of those dates?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that on the 27th of April he attended some ceremony with respect to State Day. And on the 28th, I think he visited the command of the Pristina garrison. And in the morning on the 28th, I think we moved the command post to another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that when there's some information received by the military security organs that crimes had been committed in operations that the military was involved in, there would be some investigation. Now, did you conduct any investigation as to any crime that might have occurred at Meja on the 27th or the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duties of the security organs are such that from the aspect of provided duties, they should view and monitor all the units' activities, so that the activities of the units in the area of Caragoj Valley was also followed by the security organs, and I was informed about the course of the -- that operation from the aspects of security, not, of course, the details of the action, because in view of my function, I did not need to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You know, you didn't answer the question I asked you now, but you have said in your response that you were informed about the course of that operation from the aspect of security. How were you informed about the course of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed only of the basics of that action, because my duty does not require me to know the tactics or the way a unit is used, but my duty does require me to know whether any legal conduct or criminal conduct took place on the part of members of the unit or against them perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, the question is: How? What was the means, in what way were you informed about the course of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by the competent security organ of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was this by telegram, by phone? And was this going on in the course of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was regularly informed by phone, by security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're telling me just now that you found out about it first on the evening probably of the 28th? If there are two military police battalions or platoons involved in a combat capacity in an operation, would you not be informed about that beforehand, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have to be informed, because as I stressed, there's not a single unit under the command of the chief of security, and that includes those two battalions -- not battalions, platoons of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Anyway, just clarify this for me so I could move on to the question I asked you before we got into this. Were you informed about the course of the operation regularly by phone, or were you informed about it for the first time on the evening of the -- of the 28th, when the operation was ended?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every night and every morning I received reports from the subordinate security offices. From those reports. I learned about every action, including that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it that you're now saying that you would have heard about that operation at 6.00 in the -- well, you would have heard about that operation on the morning when it began, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, nobody had the duty or the obligation to inform me as security chief about the gist of the action or the tactics on the ground. All they were obliged to do, the subordinate security organs --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which action --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. Before we continue, I have an objection. The witness is in the process of answering Mr. Stamp's question. Mr. Stamp was asking about the action, and the witness is trying to say for the second time what it is exactly that his subordinates were duty-bound to report, and Mr. Stamp is asking whether he received reports on the action, and the witness is saying for the second time that he does not receive -- he did not receive information about tactic, about the use of forces, and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, that's not what I asked him. I asked him if he'd have heard about the operation on the morning when it began and not when it ended on the 28th, in the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And he was trying to answer that, I think, Mr. Stamp. I mean, your question was not you did receive but you would have heard about, and he's explaining why he would not have heard about, as I read the answer. So I think he should complete it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're invited to complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do want to answer, and I'm saying again, in view of my position and jurisdiction, I was not the officer in the Pristina Corps Command who would have all actions, orders, and activities that units engaged in on the ground reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive information about that particular action on the morning of the -- of the -- of the 27th, when it began?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information that an action is being carried out to search for terrorists in that area, and I knew, because that area, especially the area of Smonica, was a location where hundreds of our soldiers were killed, especially on roads on the way to the border posts. I knew that much. Other details of the action, which routes the troops were going along and the tactics, et cetera, are something I didn't know. The subordinate security officer tells me usually that such-and-such an action was carried out, losses were such-and-such, illegal conduct took place or didn't take place, so many terrorists were or were not arrested, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You keep telling me that you did not have to hear about tactics and this and that, and we could have moved on very quickly. All I was asking you about was when did it come to your attention that there was an operation on the 27th and the 28th of April in Meja. And now I come back to the question I asked you later. Do you know of the military security organ being involved in any investigations of crimes that were committed by units involved in the operation in Meja area on the 27th or the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security organs would at all times - that's in their job description - inquire or investigate into criminal acts committed by members of the army or against members of the army. That is true of that particular action as well. The security officer informed me that from the viewpoint of engagement of the army, the action was carried out properly, without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So your answer is that there were no investigations, or whatever investigations there were of that operation revealed no crimes committed in the course of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security organs investigate based on clues, evidence, or reports, or intelligence that a specific crime was committed. In that specific case, we had neither evidence or reports or intelligence that a criminal act had been committed by a member of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, Meja and that general area is an area that your family is from, where you are from. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I come from the other end of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you have relatives there. You even had a family house there. And I think you testified that in gathering intelligence you even spoke to elders in the Albanian community. You had access to elders in the Albanian community. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say this again. What I said is this: In discharging my contacts and duties, I had contacts and I had operative sources among the Albanian citizenry. Mainly its separatist and terrorist segment, not among regular citizens. I also had contacts with prominent citizens, and I still have them today - and I have many Albanian friends, because that's the community I grew up in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- do you have any idea, based on your intelligence, based on your contacts with prominent citizens, based on the information from your security organs, based on the fact that you are from that area and you visited the area from time to time, including a few days before the Meja exercise by the army and the police, do you know how many people, how many Kosovo Albanians were killed in Meja area during that operation? Didn't you get any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the first I learned of the existence -- are you going to allow me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you'll answer my questions. The second question is: You have heard about people being killed in Meja during the operation to this day?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please let the witness answer that question, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer. And I repeat: The first I heard that allegedly in that operation some people were killed was when following this trial, especially the evidence whom we did not name here, except in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Were you -- and this is an -- a question that might sound rhetorical, but it needs a yes-or-no answer. Were you really serious in investigating possible crimes committed by Serbian security forces against Kosovar Albanians? Were you serious about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, always.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have information before this Court that well over 300 people, in the vicinity of 350 people reported to the Red Cross and various other organisations as missing from -- from that area at about the time of that operation. You didn't know that? That didn't come to you from your intelligence, from your family members, from your friends, from your contacts, from the prominent citizens you know, the elders you know in the community? You never had an inkling of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My communications with ethnic Albanians after 1999 came to nothing, with a few honourable exceptions. My house was burnt down after 1999, and I no longer had any information what, if anything, happened in that area. I heard it -- that it was said that some people were killed in that locality. As I said, only from following this trial, from the evidence of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I hope this has been accurately translated, but a short time ago one of the answers you gave was: "I also had contacts with prominent citizens and I still have them today, and I have many Albanian friends, because that's the community I grew up in." Was that accurately translated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was accurately interpreted. There is a number of Albanians who live in Nis, where I live now, and Albanians from other areas with whom I am in contact. But regrettably in the locality where I grew up in, where there were only 1 per cent Serbs, I no longer have any contacts with Albanians from Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Stojanovic, that answer was given in the context of being asked about that being your area where your family were from, and you said: "I come from the other end of town." And you were then asked that: "You have relatives there, you have a family house. I think you testified that you even spoke to elders in the Albanian community. You had access to elders in the Albanian community. Is that correct?" And then you gave that answer. And, you know, no one would have dreamt, I think, until you told us just now that you were talking about Albanians living far, far away from Meja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not sorry -- I'm not sure I understood your question, but I'll try to answer. I was born in Djakovica but not in a place that belongs to that area but on the other end of Djakovica, close to the bus station. I said I had contacts with prominent Albanians while I served in Kosovo and Metohija and I had quite a few friends among Albanians, and I said that to date I have contacts with individual ethnic Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, I can't even -- well, let me ask you this: Where were you? What was your job in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2001 I was commander of one brigade in the Nis garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 2002, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2002 I was chief of operations at the command of the Pristina Corps, based in Leskovac garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you were still in the army at that time. Did you not hear even a rumour circulating that hundreds of bodies were located at a place called Batajnica in Serbia? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from media reports, like any other citizen of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hear even a rumour or shall I ask you two more questions. Where were you in 2003 and 2004? What was your job in those years?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have a problem with the interpretation, I'm afraid. There's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's my fault. Sorry. The microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid you'll have to start that answer again, Mr. Stojanovic. The interpretation did not come through to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 24 March 2003 until May 2005, I occupied the post of director of the military security agency of the army of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. In that period of time, this case hadn't started yet. And in that period of time, did you hear even a rumour that many of those bodies that were found at Batajnica were the bodies of Kosovar Albanians who had been reported missing to the ICRC from Meja on the 26th -- sorry, the 27th and the 28th of April, 1999? Did you hear that in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That some bodies were found in Batajnica, I repeat, I heard through the media that exist in Serbia. I didn't hear from those media reports that the bodies originated in Meja or any other location. I simply heard that those graves were found and the press reported it in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But wasn't there a -- a debate in the media that included statements from former senior members of the VJ, including General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic, seeking to deny the army's involvement in the location of the bodies? Didn't -- didn't you know -- seeking to deny the army's involvement in these bodies that were found at Batajnica. Did you know about that, that the army and the police were being blamed for it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military security service neither at the time when I was chief in the Pristina Corps nor in the whole time I served in the army and the military security service had any intelligence or information that the execution or transportation of these bodies or any part thereof included the involvement of -- of members of the army. Why would we investigate it further if we knew well the situation in our units? And I am saying to you with full responsibility that the Army of Yugoslavia, at least on the basis of what I know from media reports and from what I know from my job as security chief in the Pristina Corps Command, the Army of Yugoslavia had no information even about the existence of bodies in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about it like any other regular citizen from -- media reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that was the question. The question was: Did you know that there was a debate in the press about denial of responsibility of the army for these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read in the press. There were many headlines about this. But I never read in any one of those reports that the army is responsible in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you read of -- did you read, sorry, of General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic making statements about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember reading any statement by General Lazarevic and General Pavkovic about it. I may be at fault for not being informed well enough, but I really haven't read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It subsequently turned out -- or scratch that. I take it that you're -- you're also saying that until this trial started, you did not know that well over 300 of those bodies found at Batajnica were positively identified to have come from Meja? You didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that from media reports I learned much earlier than this trial that there were some bodies in that location, and I said that I learned more about it from this trial and the evidence of the witness I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why can't -- why can't you just answer the question? The question was: Are you actually saying that until this trial started, you did not know that well over 300 of these bodies were positively identified as coming from Meja? Now, that requires a "yes" or a "no" answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew about the bodies found, but I didn't know that they were identified as coming from Meja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't like asking "how" questions, but I'm going to ask you: How is it -- how is it that two of your platoons could have participated in an operation in Meja, 350 people - and I must confess that I think that's a large amount of people to be coming from -- to be killed in fairly rural areas over a two-day period - could have been killed, could have been buried somewhere, disinterred, transported to Serbia without you, your security organs, your intelligence, your contacts, your friends, your Kosovar Albanian elders not even knowing a thing about it until this trial started? What was your security organ doing? Are you serious? These are many questions, but how is it that your security organ did not know about what happened in these villages in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My security organs knew very well about all the activities of the army, and I am telling you again that we had no intelligence and no reports about the existence, the alleged existence of bodies or executions that allegedly took place in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that the reason why you can't share with us how you don't know is because you very well know that there were massacres committed in those two days by forces of the -- of -- by Yugoslav -- by forces of Serb, by both the army and the police during the operation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you say, and I do not accept it in the part that involves the army. I know about that, because that was my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know about crimes of that magnitude being committed by the police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I heard no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You still haven't answered the question how it escaped you, but I have to move on. Do you have amongst the personnel in the military police Commander Kopanja? And that's in 1999. Was there a Commander Kopanja in the 52nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major Stevo Kopanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K73 said that in April 1999, when we're in Junik -- and as you well know, Junik is the northern part of the Caragoj Valley -- "we received Commander Kopanja, and he gathered the officers and gave the instruction that from now on we have to clean the area from the Albanians. Commander Kopanja clearly said that we had to send all the Albanian civilians towards Korenica, because there they were waited by MUP with a list of names of terrorists." And he said: "It was clear to me at the time that this was just a cover-up story and that the only purpose for this operation was to cleanse the village, because he could not imagine any KLA willingly going into Korenica and not fleeing the advance of our forces." Evidence of K73 is that the commanders on the ground in the military police unit, your subordinates, ordered them to expel Albanians and burn their houses. You do not know of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that commanders of the military police -- and that is something I should really know about, and I have no information about them or any other units having a task to drive out Albanians and burn their houses, and I find the statement of that witness very questionable indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt here. Sorry, General, to interrupt and to ask you this question. Now, it's once -- one thing saying you had no information or it didn't come, but you -- you had no information. But you see, you got the information through the media, through the press, as you admit yourself. And these were big incidents and occurrences, nothing small. And somebody is accusing your officers that way. I mean, you were in a position to hold some sort of investigation about it. Why was there so much inaptitude shown in this respect? I mean, this is something which I'm not able to understand. How do you -- how do you clear this position, please? Why weren't you bothered, I mean? Why didn't you go further to inquire, find the trails. All this is happening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that the Prosecutor is invoking is not something I'm aware of, and I don't know about the substance of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... No, I would confine you to something very specific. I apologise for that. But the question is: You have admitted that you read things in the press. Now, leave this document aside and leave the questions of the learned Prosecutor for a while. It is for -- it is between you and him later -- for later on. Please answer this: I mean, there were the newspapers, which you did read, and there's no denying this fact. Why weren't you disturbed on that? Why didn't you go ahead investigating? Why didn't you find out? I mean, it was nothing so small happening, if at all happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly every normal person would be upset, and I was upset, and I would try to get informed about the further course of the action and contact all my colleagues and connections throughout Kosovo and Metohija if I had known about it then. But what I'm saying to Mr. Stamp is that at that time we had not a single piece of information or indication that the members of the army had committed a murder of even one person, let alone such a large group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So you would not have investigated, even though there was, let's say, no blame, according to you, on everyone to find out what really happened. That was your territorial limits. And you did admit that you read it in the papers. So how did you react to that? I mean, in terms of action.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time, when that story appeared in the papers, I occupied one of the command posts. I was commander of the brigade and operations chief. But every normal person would take steps to get more information about what happened. However, Your Honour, I did not obtain any information that would make matters clearer to me except the information I had from media reports and from this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So you wouldn't even like to -- you wouldn't even have liked to go and visit the place with all that background and your belonging to that area and all that? You wouldn't even like to go and see if -- if it was true or if it was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would if I could like to go and visit my hometown, but I have not been able for ten years to visit the graves of my relatives and my house that was burnt down and destroyed by the terrorists, and I really can't imagine what would have to happen to make it possible for a member of the army to go to Kosovo and Metohija nowadays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In case there's any misunderstanding, we should make it clear we understand your answer to be that what you read about was the discovery of the bodies of Batajnica, and what you are saying is that you were not aware of any link at all between those bodies and the events in Meja. Now, Mr. Stamp, what else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking you about the evidence of K-89 in respect to the Meja offensive on the 27th and the 28th of April, and he said that your subordinate ordered them to expel the Albanians and burn the houses. He also testified or said that you gave orders directly to your military -- to your military police units to engage in combat activities. Is that correct? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could Mr. Stamp give us a reference first where this was said, this exact wording. Where did the witness say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, can you help?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if P2307 is sealed, P2307 in the statement of K-89 ... but he said that at paragraph 33 and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: P2 -- is that 44 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The -- the redacted version of that is P2440.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. P2440.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the record, on page 119, line 22 the question reads, if I understand English well: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... And you said that your subordinate ordered them to expel the Albanians." [Interpretation] I don't think this witness said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we now noticed K-73 and not K-89. Now, can you -- which paragraph is it, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's paragraph 33. And he was asked about paragraph 33 in the transcript, and it's closed session, so I'm being very careful, at page 3313. And basically he said - and I don't think I'm breaching anything in respect to the closed session testimony - that, to be specific, my unit, this being the entire Military Police Battalion, was subordinated directly to him. And the -- if you look at it, the question was about this witness. I think also, Your Honour, that one of the questions asked by my learned friend, Bakrac, incorporated that aspect of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you identify where this passage is that he says that orders were given?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, it -- the passage in which he says orders were given is paragraph 33 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I can't see that in the statement I'm reading at the moment, so can we go -- it must be over the page. He -- this was raised in -- in the examination-in-chief, but it wasn't about expelling Albanians. It was about stage managing events to make them look as if the KLA were responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's different from the question you've asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question I'm -- I'm asking is simply whether or not the witness gave orders to his military police units to engage in combat activities. K-33 [sic] said so, if you look at the two bits and pieces of evidence. Mr. Bakrac incorporated that question in a question that he asked. And I am just asking the witness whether he did, as really just laying the foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just look at -- look at line 18 -- 19 of page 119, which is to do with an order to expel Albanians and burn the houses. Where's -- where is the evidence for that? That's the question you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The evidence for that is page 31 -- sorry, paragraph 31 of Exhibit 2307.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, back to paragraph 31, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon, it's paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Forward to paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will read it. I will read it, if that could assist my friend. "We expelled hundreds of Albanian civilians on the first day. After the civilians left, we set fire to their houses, as this was the order." And in the context of the whole thing, you could see this was the order of Commander Kopanja, the subordinate of Major Stojanovic. And that is why I cannot understand the objection. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've now satisfied us that the question is proper. So you better formulate it again, and let's hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you give orders to your units to conduct combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we are reading something else, Your Honour, but I don't see the name Stojanovic in paragraph 42, or the name of Kopanja, Your Honour. I don't know what he's been reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question, in my view, is -- is perfectly appropriate. So please answer that question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Prosecutor has listened to my statements carefully yesterday and today and to my testimony, I said that I was never in commander of any unit of the army but that in the professional sense I proposed the use of units of the military police. If the Prosecutor's question is whether I ordered part of the units of the 52nd Military Police Battalion to do what the Prosecutor mentioned, my answer to that is "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question is: Did you order them at any time? Did you order them into combat activity, your units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never ordered them, because that was exclusively the right of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're now a little past our deadline. Is this -- but if you want to finish a chapter and it's going to be brief, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I could just get the translation from him and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you look quickly at P2297, and at page 6 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the war log of the 57th Military Police Battalion. At page 6 in English, which is page 9 in B/C/S, on the B/C/S version in e-court there's an entry for the 13th of April, 1999. Now, do you see an entry there that says: "Upon an arrival at the Morina border post"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just read that so we can confirm the translation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Upon arrival in the area of the Morina border post, we were tasked by the chief of the OB PrK to capture the border post in the village of Kamenica. The task was carried out and our troops suffered no consequences." Should I go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. Thank you. The record here is that the chief of the security sector Pristina Corps, which is you, made the order. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I did not issue -- please allow me to explain. I only conveyed the order issued by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Do you know who made this record?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like a war diary to me. It looks like the diary of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to note the date, that this is about two weeks before the incident at Meja, or the offensive at Meja. And you are saying this doesn't truly reflect what you did. Can I ask you: Do you know any reason why your subordinate, your direct subordinate, K --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one cannot impute to the witness what he did not say, and we all heard very clearly what he did say. My learned friend says "you said," and then he quotes something that the witness did not say, as we can all hear and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did he not say it doesn't truly reflect what he did? I thought he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness explained that he conveyed that it does not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's an accurate reflection of that. Please continue very quickly, Mr. Stamp, because the tape's running out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last question for today: Do you know of any reason why K-83 [sic] - and you know who he is - would want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it not 73?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K -- I beg your pardon. It's K-73.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would make untrue statements about you, his commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the right of every person to make a statement and abide by it. I answered your questions truthfully. I cannot comment on why another witness made a statement before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, Your Honours, I didn't want to interrupt, but the question is again incorrect. It says here: Why would this witness say something about his commander, but this witness never said that Stojanovic was his immediate commander. And the witness explained who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has already told us that he actually conveyed this order. The interpretation that Mr. Stamp is suggesting is one that is open to him to suggest. What we accept about all this will depend on our judgement on the evidence. There's nothing wrong with the way in which that cross-examination was conducted. We'll have to interrupt here, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid there's a couple of things to be dealt with. Mr. Fila, the exhibit you referred to latterly in your cross-examination, 2D391, where -- which related to Vasiljevic and the notebook, we refused the admission of that exhibit recently in an order. The witness here has no knowledge of it, so for the avoidance of any doubt on the matter, that document is not admitted in any -- to any extent at all. Mr. Lukic, Mr. Stamp mentioned it and I -- earlier this morning, and I told you that -- or I said then that -- that the matter was being dealt with urgently, that is the notification of further details of your witnesses in terms of the order we made in October. There is still no response to that, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is in the system, Your Honour. It should be available today, during the day. It's filed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. And I take it the other matter you raised with us has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We got, with your help the permission to visit our client tomorrow, although it's not working day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now there's also outstanding - if the tape runs out, too bad. These are administrative matters and not essential to the evidence in the case. There is an issue over the interposition of a witness on Monday. Mr. Stamp, what's your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no objection to that. If the Defence could find a way that we could proceed in the normal way, I think it would be better, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- if there are restraints that they have to abide by, I accede to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We -- we agree with that, Mr. Bakrac, that it would be far more suitable on this occasion to complete Mr. Stojanovic before moving to another witness. I think the timing of your next witness is such that he would not occupy the whole of two days. Now, whether you can work out a scheme with -- with the Prosecutor to try to avoid interposing the next witness is -- is something we would ask you to explore. If you can't, then there's no objection to you interposing him, but we would prefer you to try to get round it in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must know from the Prosecutor exactly how much time he still has for his cross-examination and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you -- but you can deal with that after we've risen. Mr. Stojanovic, you -- you would normally be told to be back here on Monday morning at 9.00; however, there's a possibility that a different arrangement will be made. That will -- if it changes, you'll be told. But unless you hear something to the contrary, you should be back here at 9.00 on Monday morning and you should be very careful over the weekend to ensure that you avoid discussion of the case or any of the evidence in the case with anyone. You must confine yourself to other subjects and discuss in no way the evidence in this case or any part of it. We'll rise now and sit at 9.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
